#4097. Talking Point: With Big Walk, The AI-In-Game-Dev Debate Just Got A Lot Murkier

"The line must be drawn here! This far, no further!"

Please forgive the Captain Picard First Contact quote (it's been a couple of weeks since Patrick Stewart's death and only now can I mention his most famous character without welling up) - I promise it's relevant as an illustration of an admirable, principled stance.

In the Borg, good ol' Jean-Luc had a well-defined enemy to engage, with the threat of humanity's assimilation providing a pretty clear line between good and bad. There are larger philosophical questions about the hive mind and our aversion to Star Trek's cube-riding automatons, but for the purposes of this article, let's assume we're all in agreement: Borg=baaad.

Back in the real world, though, that line between right and wrong often isn't so easy to define. Today there'll be a lot of commentators in the video game space, players and developers alike, longing for a better understanding of another encroaching, all-consuming entity.

House House's belated disclosure that LLMs were used during the development of indie hit Big Walk pours fuel on an already raging debate and brings questions over permissible AI use in game dev right back into the discourse - specifically the differences between generative AI for player-facing audio-visual assets and writing versus coding and other less obvious uses.

News Big Walk Devs Issue Statement Over AI Usage

This latest flashpoint followed a statement released by a subset of IGF Award jurors explaining why they won't be voting for games developed using any form of generative AI.

Last year, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — which swept The Game Awards with nine wins from 13 nominations — raised similar questions after the Indie Game Awards disqualified Sandfall Interactive's game upon discovering AI had been used in the development pipeline.

I've voiced my distaste for GenAI, and it remains a massive no-no - professionally and personally. I'm fortunate to not have corporate overlords mandating its use around these parts, which certainly isn't the case for some other outlets, nor for many creatives in the gaming space. The gulf in quality between the human-written word and generated bilge is still enormous and easily identifiable, and for now, the same is broadly true of GenAI visual artwork, too.

What this Big Walk situation highlights, however, is how difficult it can be to discern in other places, and the increasing pull it has on even the most principled developers.

Talking Point Does It Bother You That Big Games Companies Are Using GenAI?

The phrase gets bandied around a lot, but it's fair to call Big Walk a proper 'critical darling'. It garnered "Universal Acclaim" back in August, with an impressive 91 Metascore. Alex gave it a "Great" 8/10 after reviewing the Switch 2 version for us - technical hiccups took the shine off it for him, but he still loved the co-op experience. And by September it was already Nile's GOTY.

As someone who didn't play Big Walk at launch, its place in my GOTY-catch-up priorities may have shifted, but wherever you land on the GenAI spectrum, the consensus among critics and players is as unanimous as it gets: Big Walk is an excellent video game.

There are many issues to consider — not least where AI use crosses from tool to theft — but an important one relates to how this game in particular has had a profound effect on many players. Rejecting something flagged as 'suspicious' on principle is easy, especially with so many brilliant games releasing each week. But something you've played already and internalised and loved? From a dev team you respect?

For some, this revelation will feel like when a beloved artist/actor/writer/musician is revealed to be problematic, but we're not talking about illegal behaviour or allegations here.

If House House's statement is to be taken at face value, the team used a chatbot to find a solution to a coding issue with Unity, the third-party engine the game is built on. People online with real chops have already investigated the specifics of House House's single example:

took me 3 hours but I figured out the “URP culling shadowcasters behind the camera” issue House House cites in their disclosure. This culls immediately when the object is off-camera, but modifying the culling params with a custom frustrum is straightforward

this needs cleaning up but is basically the gist

This was a terrible use of 3 hours, but I know just a bit more about how to do something cool. I’m sympathetic to them wanting to ship something good but AI rots your damn brain

That's the one example the devs offer in their statement, and the language around further usage feels vague. The impression it gives is of a team searching for a solution to a specific problem using common tools, as opposed to vibe-coding huge swathes of the game.

Now, I've never programmed anything in my life, but I can appreciate that efficient code must be an art in itself. Is it any less of an art because that code is invisible to players? Then again, to me, generating great chunks of game code feels very different from using an LLM to squash a bug or find a solution when third-party documentation fails. Is one usage as 'bad' as the other, or is this slippery slope, gateway-drug territory?

(Perhaps if any programmers are reading, they'd like to share thoughts in the comments - as the headline says, this is very much a talking point and I'm keen to explore with as much nuance as the internet will permit.)

My point is that seeing exactly where to draw that line is increasingly difficult when AI tools of all types become ubiquitous. A blanket rejection of anything inevitably now means excluding not just an increasing number of games, but also artistically significant, important ones.

And with executives like former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser advocating the use of AI for indie teams to improve workflow, it's also easy to understand how a developer might turn to the tech. The whole topic is getting greyer by the day, much to the pleasure of evangelists, I'm sure.

Like it or not, this situation forces AI sceptics to reconcile their positive feelings for the game. House House estimates "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code" has any trace of generative AI, but to paraphrase a certain Starfleet captain again, "How much does it take before it becomes wrong, hmm?" That is the question.

For some players who simply don't care, it's a non-issue. Some may reluctantly cut the game from their lives and GOTY lists. I suspect that others, though, disappointed or otherwise, will start reconsidering where they personally draw the AI line.

And if House House hadn't disclosed this, would anyone have ever known? I'd guess not. And if a celebrated indie team turned to AI as a problem-solver, how many other devs aren't disclosing similar usage? And how many sure-as-hell won't do so after this?

Lots of questions, no clear answers, just murk. How unsatisfying. I've heard 'ends-justify-means' sentiments online — 'hey, if the game is good, does it matter?' — which feel unsavoury given the documented, quantifiable damage AI is doing to the games industry and the wider world. It's that damage which has IGF jurors abstaining from voting for Big Walk this year: an understandable, admirable stance.

Which leads us to one final question: What would Captain Picard do?

Naturally, he'd call everyone into the Observation Lounge for a big old meeting in a calm, civilised manner, that's what. Conference.

Let us know below if this revelation changes your relationship with the game or where you draw the line when it comes to generative AI in its various forms.

I’m not a game dev but a software engineer with over 15 years of end-to-end more than just full stack software development experience who helped build up 2 successful startups with my own hand written code, no matter the coding language, backend, front end, infrastructure as code.

I’ve started to increasingly use AI because in today’s world it would burn you out to do anything without AI with all the pressure coming from needing to survive as a business.

My own rule is simply to use AI only to the capacity that ensures you have full control and AI doesn’t take over, and not in a way that replaces Human Resources but improves efficiency. In art this is difficult to achieve, but for coding it is simple.

1) If it’s some quick one-time tedious type of work (e.g. migrating to a new system), AI can be immensely helpful, you only need to review the end-result/output. I find the use of AI okay if you are capable of ensuring quality output and review it.

I had AI write scripts to do several types of migration work where it would take me weeks to learn all the tiny bits and unknowns, then write all the code. I used to do it all by hand and it is thankless work where you learn a lot of things you will never apply again in your life. Perfect scenario for AI to just do it. It can research everything needed and think of unknowns you couldn’t think of. Once the work is done, throw the scripts away because migration is done. Weeks of work reduced to a mere few hours. Instead I can focus on more fun parts of my job.

2) if its production level code that impacts user experience, I feel you should only use AI for assistance to improve and not to build. You need full control. We had an instance in the company somebody wrote the entire microservice via AI in a way he was incapable of debugging without AI. One part of it I had to rewrite completely by hand to fix it. They had no clue what they were doing and it could have been a disaster.

Unfortunately, I personally have come across too many lazy developers that make me prefer AI written code over their code, because AI simply codes better, more structured, can follow design patterns properly.

If you are unable to clearly envision the expected logic you intend to write, the expected design patterns used, don’t use AI. Learn first.

This brings me to 3) using AI to improve your skills is an extremely powerful tool. I told a friend to have AI teach him design patterns since I have no time for doing that, but he can always cross check with me. He has never improved so fast in his own hand-written creations before AI.

— Now I’ve tried using AI in various ways for coding and one thing for sure is that you need to be extremely good in giving boundaries and directions. Basically the correct “prompt”, and you can only do that if you have enough experience and skills yourself to control AI in that way. And you can never get there if you just let AI do all the work. It makes a lot of mistakes.

Now if I had to not worry about money, I would use AI far less and only for code reviews or learning, basically jsut as “feedback”, not a producer. But that’s not something I can afford, especially in a world where all employers now expect you to use AI to improve cost-efficiency.

Maybe not a common take, or a popular one, but I'm not a developer, yet I've been able to do amazing things with AI that I never could have without it. I have always had ideas and never been able to do anything with them because I lack the skill to code, and the time/desire to learn.

Since picking up Claude Code less than a year ago I've made several small games for myself that were terrible and I abandoned, but I've also been able to make some great stuff:

All of these projects are open source, on my github, and I will never charge for them, so I have the luxury of saying if you don't like it, don't use it. But I can sympathize with people who CAN code and are being forced to work faster not smarter on commercial projects, or losing their jobs altogether because 1 developer can do the work of 3, with the quality of none.

At work I've been able to (with my CEO's blessing) teach an AI agent how to fix 80% of the issues we see regularly to the point where over half of my daily work is done now with fully deterministic code, written by an AI agent, and the rest is triaged and investigated before I ever see it. Our time to resolution has gone down, and customer satisfaction has gone up, and we still send every communication by hand. None of the code is user facing, and none is supported by our dev team, so it's only to benefit our support staff.

I'm absolutely against using AI to replace people, whether it's in development, design, art, writing, communication, or anywhere else, but I'm a huge proponent of using it to enable your team to hand-off the time consuming, repetitive tasks to agents and focus on the things that the love about their job instead.

@dartmonkey I'm an embedded software engineer who has dabbled a bit in AI-assistent use in the context of my work. I'd say at the moment I have a "middle of the road" stance on AI usage in this form. I've seen the advantages and disadvantages of using AI for code generation/fix/support and I acknowledge both the opportunities and threats that AI present.

In my experience, the code that an engineer writes is a means to an end, a way to implement a certain logic concept into something that actually works. As such, I consider my core work to be the conceptual logic I think of, whereas the actual coding part is merely a necessary task to fulfil that logic. It's no surprise then that code generation has been used for decades already in software engineering, be it model-based or low-code or whatever that I'm not even aware of. Though most of those solutions were not very smart, the generation works based on a very strict logic and it's the engineer task to make sure that logic translates into correct code. In this context, using AI to generate code seems merely a new iteration of the same concept, but now it's smarter. It uses the experience of thousands of software engineers to try and generate the correct code based on the prompt. A different way to achieve the same result.

Now, some would say that writing the most optimized, efficiently running and easily maintainable code is also an art in itself. That may be true, but history has also shown that humans engineers are phenomenally bad at achieving that result consistently (which explains why code generation is even a thing). We're reliant on other, more experienced engineers to show us how to achieve those code quality goals, the best design patterns and the best practices. And that in turn makes the code we write only as good as the teachers that taught us. Now compare that with using AI, which will eventually (MAJOR caveat there, "eventually" is doing a lot of heavy lifting) be trained on the best quality code, best design patterns and best practices of hundreds of thousands software engineers. That's a huge win. It's a good result, especially in the context of "just writing the code". If the engineer creates the correct design, the AI only needs to generate the best possible code to make that design a reality. Based on this view, I do not consider AI use to generate, fix or optimize code an issue.

@dartmonkey But I'd like to reframe the concept to something you as a writer can better relate to. How do you feel about the following scenario. A writer is struggling with a paragraph in a certain text, even after multiple drafts they are not satisfied. Eventually, they contact a fellow writer and ask the very simple question "how would you write this part"? Perfectly normal, right? But how about that writer uses an AI to ask the same question. Instead of getting one suggestion from a known source, they get the combined response of over thousands of writers. Sure, these are anonymous sources and might not have given this response explicitly, but the end result is much the same, I think.

This is similar to the coding scenario, I believe. The question becomes, what is your core output as a writer. The message you want to convey, or the way you present that message. Now, I can see how for writing that presentation is much more important that the coding is for achieve a logic result; calling the actual writing of a text "a means to an end" for a message is going too far. But, I think considering this view has merit.

And so, with the use of AI in any context, I think the way AI is utilized is very important in determining the "morality" of its use. There's a huge difference between asking an AI to "write a positive review about this game" and "reword this paragraph to make it sound more neutral". Same as there's a huge different between asking an AI to "make a game where an electrician jumps on platforms" and "make the physics of this jump routine more natural".

#4096. Poll: Xbox Turns 25 This Week, But Which Console Generation Had The Best Launch Titles?

This Sunday, Xbox will celebrate 25 years of great games and console experiences. Without giving away just how ancient we are, Fraser and I have been Xbox players since the beginning, enjoying each new generation of Xbox consoles and the games that launched alongside them.

With November 15th drawing closer, we thought we'd look back on each generation's launch lineup and ask for your verdict: which Xbox console had the best launch titles?

Was it the original Xbox, with Halo: Combat Evolved, Project Gotham Racing, and Fuzion Frenzy? How about the Xbox 360, with Condemned: Criminal Origins, Kameo: Elements of Power, and Call of Duty 2? Perhaps the Xbox One, with Ryse: Son of Rome, Dead Rising 3, and Forza Motorsport 5? Or is it the Xbox Series X|S, with Gears Tactics, Forza Horizon 4, and Sea Of Thieves?

We all have our favourite games from each console generation, but which one had the best launch lineup? That's for you to decide by voting in the poll below. Before you do, though, here's a closer look at each Xbox generation's launch titles:

On this page: Poll: Xbox Turns 25 This Week, But Which Console Generation Had The Best Launch Titles?

So, now you know which games launched with which Xbox consoles, and all that's left to do is vote! I reckon I can probably guess which console the PX community will favour, but who knows? Get voting!

#4095. Helldivers 2 boss can "absolutely see" making a game parody of generative AI, but it would need to be "quirky" rather than "doom-laden"

Arrowhead's chief creative officer Johan Pilestedt can well imagine the Helldivers studio developing a videogame that satirises or parodies today's generative AI technology. The game in question wouldn't be a Helldivers project, however, and Pilestedt says it would need to be relatively upbeat, rather than an exercise in feverish despair. This seems like a tall order right now, at least while Tim Sweeney still has access to Twitter.

"AI has been worth parodying since the ‘80s, and I can absolutely see a game where you’re stuck in a world with an AI overlord that’s basically a deity," Pilestedt told me during an interview on the company's future. "But the Automatons already cover our robot enemy needs in Helldivers 2, so if we went there, it would be a new title, and we’d want to frame it in a quirky, fun way rather than a doom-laden one."

The aim to keep things light is consistent, of course, with how Helldivers approaches satire. "Not everyone gets it, but plenty of players love playing along with the joke," Pilestedt commented elsewhere in our chatathon, with regard to how Helldivers portrays fascism. "The humor doesn't hide the message, it delivers it."

While robotic, Helldivers 2's Automatons aren't a commentary on generative AI. They're broadly a spoof of Soviet Russia, red star imagery and all, if Soviet Russia had happened to be populated by Terminators. Based on the secessionist planet of Cyberstan, the Automatons are led by a group of Cyborgs who are waging war partly out of revenge for Super Earth's efforts to "euthanise" them. Still, perhaps there's scope to patch in more present-day parallels and upgrade the Automatons from cosy T-1000 analogues into something redolent of, say, Krafton's plans to use game data for unpiloted weapon systems.

Any satire of genAI Arrowhead make would need to reckon with the fact that Arrowhead appear open to making use of the technology, within limits. “I find that anything that is [an] AI-related debate in the games industry ends up being on both ends of the spectrum," Arrowhead CEO Shams Jorjani told The Game Business in an interview last year. "Either we have Square Enix executives talking about 77% being automated through QA, or we have developers who feel that... the very fabric of their being is being threatened and therefore all AI is bad AI. Maybe could it be that reality is somewhere in the middle?"

Jorjani contrasted fears about job losses to generative AI with less anxious reaction to older automation middleware such as Simplygon, while conceding that Simplygon isn't on the same "massive scale" as generative AI tools. He also stressed that "we need to make sure that we're not stealing people's intellectual property and rights".

Pilestedt didn't share his own opinions about generative AI during our conversation - in his defence, I didn't ask for them specifically. He did, however, talk about why Arrowhead's current unannounced project isn't Helldivers 3 - briefly, they don't want to "reset" the momentum of Helldivers 2.

#4093. Rockstar developer union could end up over 1,600 workers strong and encompass nearly all UK staff below senior management, IWGB claim

Organisers say a successful vote would create "the biggest recognised union in the UK games sector"

As we've previously covered, a vote on recognition of a union made up of UK-based Rockstar Games devs is set to take place around GTA 6's console launch on November 19th. The Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB) union, whom the Rockstar staff are working with in their efforts to organise, have now revealed just how many workers the Rockstar could end up encompassing if the recognition vote is successful. It's not a small number.

As reported by Game File, when asked to put a number on their claim that the vote could result in "the biggest recognised union in the UK games sector", the IWGB said that the union’s bargaining unit would be made up of more than 1,600 workers. That, according to the union, is nearly everyone at Rockstar's UK studios below the director level. The director level's typically corpospeak for senior management, or the point at which you go from regular staff to the lowest rungs of the exec ladder which leads all the way up to the biggest of gold-plated desks.

Naturally, this UK Rockstar union won't include Rockstar staff based in other studios across the world, including the US and India. Recent reporting from Bloomberg cited Rockstar's total staff number as being over 4,700 people in 12 places across the globe.

The UK union recognition votes will be held from November 12th, a week before GTA 6's console launch, and November 26th.

"For me, this vote comes down to ensuring employees at Rockstar get honesty and openness surrounding the decisions that affect them," Rockstar Game Workers Union Committee Member Shanti Easton-Steel said in a press release issued by IWBG earlier this week. "When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."

Also set to come to a head around the time GTA 6 plops onto consoles is the employment tribunal which has seen Rockstar and the IWGB butt heads over the former's decision to fire 34 mostly UK-based staffers last year. Rockstar have accused the fired staff of risking the leaking of confidential info while posting on a Discord server set up by union organisers. The IWGB have accused Rockstar of being motivated by a desire to union bust.

World of Warcraft: Forever has suffered a bit of a PvP debacle since its official release last week, with faction imbalance drama hitting a high – but Blizzard is working to remedy it.

Yes, the studio is well aware of the issue – one that, if you're out of the loop yourself, has seen folks complaining about everything from too many Horde players to unplayable PvP realms – and a recent update on its official forums proves as much. "It's vitally important that the PvP rulesets in WoW: Forever have balanced factions where both factions vie for supremacy," it begins, and I'd certainly agree there. "Creating memories of epic victories and stunning defeats that we all remember for years to come," after all, is what it's all about. Blizzard says that that ideal balance, however, isn't there – even if it is "close," so to speak: "While even the most extreme case in a region is currently at roughly a 55/45 split, that is not as close as we want it to be." In turn, the developers are rolling out some changes… and, unsurprisingly, restrictions.

"To better set the stage for the neck-and-neck conflicts we all want, we've adjusted the character creation system to better recognize the overall state of faction balance in each region's PvP rulesets, rather than what may feel like snapshots of points in time," Blizzard explains. "Our goal is to bring things as close to a 50/50 faction balance as possible." And, yes, this means you can't create characters willy-nilly.

"In the short term, that means that it will become increasingly difficult to create characters on the more populous faction in each region – currently Horde on North American PvP rulesets or Alliance in EU Roleplay-PvP," as the devs say. "As everyone settles and shifts, these may flip to the other side," though. It might be a bit annoying to Horde hopefuls in the US or those who prefer teaming up with the Alliance in Europe, but it makes sense.

In Blizzard's own words, "We recognize that while restrictions are in place, it can be frustrating to not be able to start playing a specific faction in that moment, but this is a necessary trade-off for the long-term health of the ruleset, especially early on when guilds are being established and rivalries developed." The current imbalance isn't sustainable, basically, not to mention all of the controversy it's sparking.

Blizzard concludes that "World of Warcraft: Forever's PvP is at its best when the Alliance and Horde are on equal footing, and we are dedicated to helping maintain that balance so that we can all witness battles at the epic scale that has made WoW: Forever PvP so memorable thus far" – and I'm hopeful, personally. All of the commotion has put me off dipping my toes into PvP, but Blizzard's adjustments might just change that.

Here's hoping we see better balance between the factions in PvP in the days to come in both the US and EU – it's evident that Blizzard's on the case, at least.

#4091. Mouse Work, The Switch 2 Game Using Joy-Con Mouse Controls, Arrives This December

Update [Tue 10th Nov 2026, 11:35pm]: Nitrome has now officially announced Mouse Work will be arriving for Switch 2 on 7th December 2026.

It's described as the ultimate showcase for the system's mouse controls, and will include a "massive 8-10 hour campaign solo" or you can bring a crew with you for a co-op experience. This includes 1-4 players locally and online via GameShare.

This title will set you back $19.99 / £15.99 and pre-orders are now live on the eShop. Nitrome has also shared a new trailer, which you can check out above.

Original Story: Remember Mouse Work? It was announced by developer Nitrome for the Switch 2 just a few months before the system's launch and requires you to use mouse controls to complete all sorts of fun and challenging jobs.

We've not got an update about this title since last year, but it looks like it's finally on the way. According to a listing that has recently appeared on the Japanese Nintendo Store and eShop, it will be arriving this holiday season on 7th December 2026 for 2,200 yen.

The translated description notes how the campaign is 10 hours across more than 50 unique stages. You'll also be able to participate in local and online multiplayer, including GameShare support. When we hear more about the local release, we'll provide an update.

Nitrome has previously released games such as Bomb Chicken and Shovel Knight Dig on the original Switch. Are you excited for its new game on Switch 2? Let us know in the comments.

#4089. New Details Revealed About The Physical Edition Of GTA 6 For Xbox Series X|S

Double-sided poster, shipping dates & more

Everyone already knows about the code-in-a-box situation for GTA 6's physical edition on Xbox Series X|S and PS5, but we've also come to learn a few extra details in recent days about what to expect from the boxed copy of the game.

So, when you open up GTA 6 for Xbox Series X|S in physical form, you'll be presented with a code that will allow you to redeem the game on the Microsoft Store - essentially converting your physical purchase into a digital one.

Rockstar Games mentioned a shipping date of November 12th for the physical version a few days ago, but we've spotted some retailers saying they'll start shipping on the 11th instead, while a very small number of people even seem to have their copy already.

Once you've got the physical version in your hands, you'll be able to preload GTA 6 in full, although you can technically also do that from tonight by installing the game via the Xbox mobile app.

As you can also see from the tweet above, the physical edition is now confirmed to come with a double-sided A3 poster (at least if you buy from certain retailers). This poster appears to include the game's main artwork along with some character art on the back, so that's at least a nice little bonus to ease the pain of a disc-less release.

But what about a map? Well, Rockstar Games is handling the map a bit differently this time around, making a digital version available to download for free at launch. Alternatively, physical maps will be available to buy from the Rockstar Store "shortly after launch" for $0.99, but we reckon those will be in extreme demand and quickly sell out.

Of course, none of this really changes the fact that the physical edition of GTA 6 is kinda pointless for any platform as things stand, but it does at least make for a good display piece, and it'll be popular for gifting purposes this Christmas.

What's even weirder about this is that Rockstar is supporting GTA 6's launch with various other physical releases, such as an official soundtrack album and all kinds of merch, but it seems there's little hope for a disc version right now.

#4088. GTA 6 PS5 Pro Features Revealed, 30fps Target on Both Consoles

Improved clarity and ray traced shadows on PS5 Pro

Rockstar Games has today revealed what sort of benefits playing GTA 6 on a PS5 Pro will provide.

No matter whether you play on a base PS5 or a PS5 Pro, though, the game will target 30 frames-per-second, a new post on the developer's website confirms:

Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants.

The improvements are slim on PS5 Pro; the article mentions "improved clarity" thanks to PSSR, and there'll be ray traced shadows that are only available on the upgraded console.

There is no 60fps mode, or even a 40fps mode for GTA 6. This also applies to the Xbox Series X|S versions.

Guide GTA 6 Release Times and Preload: When Can You Start Playing?

The blog post then talks up the game's use of the PS5 DualSense controller, making use of haptic feedback, far better audio, and improved load times. It concludes by calling PS5 the best place to play GTA 6.

As of today, the game is available to preload worldwide on PS5 ahead of the full 19th November launch. Please refer to our GTA 6 Release Times and Preload guide for more information. How do you feel about there being no 40fps or 60fps performance modes in GTA 6? Let us know in the comments below.

"We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world," House House says

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Indie darling Big Walk has found itself in hot water as developer House House admits to previously undisclosed AI usage "in the final stretch" of its co-op game's development, which it says touched "well under 0.1%" of the code.

This has surfaced after a statement from a group of jurors on the Independent Games Festival (IGF) was shared on Bluesky, acknowledging the "significant increase in the number of submitted games developed with generative AI tools" for the upcoming awards show. The group – which doesn't speak for IGF leadership or every juror – outlines the many issues with AI, from "ecological harms" to "cognitive and psychological harms to its users" and "harms to labor and worker power in creative fields," and says "we are declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity." That includes everything, be it artwork, voice acting, or indeed, code.

It's code that Big House developer House House now admits that it used large language models for help with in a public statement shared on the game's FAQ page. The devs acknowledge that "a version" of this statement was sent to the IGF as "a suggested part" of its submission, but say that the reason there's no AI disclosure on its Steam page is because Valve "does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage," which is what House House used the tech for.

"In the final stretch of Big Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," its statement begins. "In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code – we'd estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

"The primary use case for House House's use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code."

The devs give an example of one use of AI. After running into an issue where the game was slowing down significantly at sunrise and sunset, they were unable to find a fix themselves or after asking an engineer working for game engine Unity. "Finally," House House says, the team asked an AI chatbot instead.

"After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked," House House says. "This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP [Universal Render Pipeline]."

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

Despite the studio's usage of the tech, House House says "this is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal." It continues with an apology: "We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalization of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable.' We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologize that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards.

"Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

As you might expect, fans aren't exactly happy. Looking at Big Walk's reviews on Steam, there's been a huge spike in negative feedback posted today – compared to just one negative review yesterday and three the day before, at the time of writing, today's reviews are just 36% positive, with 156 giving it a big, red thumbs down, with a number also indicating that they've refunded the title.

"Undisclosed use of AI to finish their game. This is a misrepresentation of the quality and effort put into an otherwise wonderful game. What a disappointment," reads one. "I wish I could still love this game. It is maddening," says another. "I find the lack of AI disclosure disturbing, upsetting, and very disappointing. If it hadn't already been a few months since I bought this, I would be making a point to refund it," another writes.

I suspect we'd be seeing many more refunds if it wasn't for the fact that this information has only just surfaced five months since Big Walk's launch, at a point where the majority of players are likely well past the date – and playtime – that would make them eligible to get their money back on Steam.

As disappointing as the news is for many, Big Walk is far from the only well-loved game to find itself in the center of a, uh, Big Backlash for AI usage. Last year, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 saw two of its wins at The Indie Game Awards (including Game of the Year) revoked after what appeared to be AI-generated textures were discovered (and then quietly, and quickly, patched out) of the J'RPG. Crimson Desert similarly patched out a bunch of AI-generated assets after its launch earlier this year.

GTA 6 CEO says AI will make creating games easier, but "making a big hit" will be as hard as ever: "Hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

#4086. Splendid Junji Ito-inspired RPG World of Horror is now 20% more horrible, thanks to a free PC update with extra gods, locations, and wounds

This hole was already made for me, but now it's a fair bit wider and deeper

Excellent apocalypse RPG World of Horror has just received a sizeable free update, As Below So Above, adding no less than two Old Godly invasions for you to identify and thwart. One of these additional cosmic disasters involves four cults summoning their fave abominations at the same time. I picture them forming a shaky barbershop quartet on the skyline, while stamping the streets to mush. Damn it, Ath-Yolazsth – you're leading again!

Also in As Below So Above: more "enemies, mysteries, characters, items, spells, curses, and injuries", together with "a large batch of quality-of-life features and bug fixes". I can only applaud the vicious disconnect of listing "injuries" alongside "quality-of-life". These will be the most polished and ergonomic grievous wounds you've ever had! The experience will flow like your gushing blood!

This is the Junji Ito-inspired game's largest update yet, according to developers panstasz and publishers Ysbryd. It makes the game 20% bigger, though surely no mere percentage can ever encapsulate the creatures and forces that slumber on the other side of the mortal veil.

"Two never-before-seen manifestations of the Old Gods raise the stakes," explains the press release. "IKT-YOSIS, THE FIRST NIGHTMARE, sleeps in a gargantuan chamber beneath the mountains. With each ritual performed to wake him, the world above slowly reshapes itself and brings strange weather with it." You'll need to keep tabs on forecasts, if you want to get ahead of the elements. As for "THE WAR FOR SHIOKAWA", this "adds an extra level of terror, with four cults summoning their eldritch masters simultaneously to plunge the town into pure evil."

It's just as well there are three new puny human protagonists to continue the battle against these cyclopean trouble-makers: Kiriko, who knows her way around a Tarot deck, Satoshi, a seasoned hiker, and Makoto, a school AV club member. You'll also be able to enlist 10 additional allies and learn about them care of a reworked conversation system, which trips at random between investigations.

There's a new location, the Mountains, alongside 60 extra events, 19 enemies, three challenges, and 30 items. And let's not forget the Scenario Mode, which plays host to self-contained yarns set before the main game. The first of these Worldlets of Horror is a hunt for three students lost in the woods, with a variety of endings.

Lots of numbers! And while much of this may break your mind, none of it will break your mods. There's a new modding system that's backwards compatible with everything made for the 1.0 version.

Unfamiliar with World of Horror? Here is Alice Bee's review (RPS in peace): "Repetitive combat in World Of Horror can't entirely mar a unique, stylish and layered horror adventure that makes you want to play more the more that you play."

There are rumblings in the world of Gordon Freeman. No, it's not the sudden release of Half-Life 3, but instead another leak of apparent code from a version of Half-Life 2: Episode 3, revealing details of what Valve was experimenting in the latent follow-up.

The Valve-dedicated social media account GabeFollower posted the findings. They posted a screenshot of the source code for Episode 3, showing a couple of insights into the game's development.

The big takeaways this go round lie in the weapons, where you can find evidence of offensive items the Blobulator and the Weaponizer. The former was actually demonstrated by Valve back when the company actually did showcases and promoted upcoming games, around 2007 and 2008, where it was teased as part of Episode 3.

It's essentially a giant blob of mercury that you could use to attack or trap enemies. It could be separated up into different shapes and molded to suit various needs, and all pieces would revert back together like the T-1000. One drawback is that it's somewhat sentient, and would attack you in the wrong circumstance, so you had to be careful.

Of course, Episode 3 never came out, and the studio went through a number of different versions of the next installment of Half-Life between then and now. The tech behind the Blobulator eventually found its way into Portal 2, for the Mobility Gels.

The Weaponizer is far more mysterious. We still don't really know what its purpose would've been, and Valve isn't exactly forthcoming. The date range on the code places it around 2008, making it the first version of Episode 3, eventually thrown away by Gabe Newell and company for another iteration.

More source code provides ammunition for modders to build a Half-Life 3 of their own that perhaps resembles what Valve was hoping to achieve. Absent something more substantial from the mysterious halls of the Steam creators, that remains our best bet for another chapter in the story.

#4083. EA execs choosing Star Wars Battlefront 3 over Mass Effect 5 was the main factor in BioWare's demise, according to report

Corporate chair shuffling and the Mass Effect studio's recent struggles may also have played roles

The postmortem on BioWare, following their shuttering by EA this month, points to the publisher's preference to back Star Wars Battlefront 3 over Mass Effect 5 as the main factor in the demise of the beloved RPG developer. That's according to Bloomberg, who also report that a couple of other factors likely also had some influence.

The Bloomberg report paints EA's position as being one of a company caught between spending a bunch of money on a Star Wars shooter-shaped rock and a hard place with a sign that read Mass Effect 5. Disney reportedly swooped in to offer the publishers the opportunity to make Star Wars Battlefront 3 around the time EA were, as a result of being saddled with debt as part of the leveraged buyout which saw the Saudi government and private equity take them over, looking to not to spend as much cash.

So, Star Wars and Mass Effect became a decision of whether Star Wars or Mass Effect would be the better bet to stick projected hundreds of millions of dollars on. The suits, quelle surprise really, went for the series that currently sits just below powerhouse money-maker Winnie the Pooh on Wikipedia's list of the highest-grossing media franchises. Battlefront 3's development reportedly hasn't even kicked off yet, but it's got that safe and predictable big name to it, and will be a shooter to nestle among EA's treasured flotilla of gun and ball games, rather than an RPG.

Bloomberg add that that BioWare's well-documented up and down record with game releases since Mass Effect: Andromeda began a skid which Anthem only made worse and Dragon Age: The Veilguard couldn't arrest also played a role. Potentially also in the mix was some corporate chair and nameplate switching among EA's execs this summer, which saw EA Sports-linked suits David Tinson and Cam Weber promoted while reported BioWare advocate Laura Miele was sidelined via promotion from overseeing EA's non-sports studios to a gig based around helping big boss Andrew Wilson pursue "strategic growth opportunities beyond EA's core business".

For what it's worth, an EA spokesperson told Bloomberg the company "collectively" decided to shoot BioWare into space "following months of planning, review, and analysis, including careful consideration of evolving business conditions, industry dynamics, and our long-term priorities".

And so, BioWare's body has been sent to the stars, while Respawn and DICE look set to make Battlefront 3. There is a bit of depressing irony in EA deciding to go for the perceived safe bet of a big name licensed game over taking some risk on a game that'd come without Disney as a rights-holding middleman. This is, after all, the company which in 2022 ditched governing body Fifa as the namesake and licensing partner of their very successful football games, choosing the risk of going it alone with a lesser brand EA would have more direct control over and ownership of rather than sticking with an established big name juggernaut.

Then again, you could probably call EA's soccer games something like 'Hey, you, person reading this: the (insert year here) football game you're looking at thinks your face is ugly and your haircut's stupid' and they'd still fly off the shelves.

#4082. Unknown 9 Dev Being Shut Down Two Years After Disaster PS5 Launch

Do you remember Unknown 9: Awakening? Published by Bandai Namco, the story-driven stealth-action title had a fairly hard marketing push ahead of its release back in October 2024 — but it was labelled a "failure" just months after its launch.

It was a commercial disaster, selling way below expectations, and developer Reflector Entertainment was subsequently hit with layoffs, before revealing that it would be put to work on an existing Bandai Namco property.

Bandai Namco itself had acquired the Canadian studio in 2020. We don't know how much the deal was worth, but it's now been confirmed that the publisher ate an "extraordinary" 3.5 billion yen loss on Unknown 9. That's approximately $22 million / £16 million / €21 million.

That's according to Bandai Namco's own press release, which also confirms Reflector Entertainment's closure.

"After comprehensively considering future business plans, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation, the Company has decided to discontinue Reflector’s business, dissolve and liquidate it," the company writes.

It's a brutal end for a team that has seemingly been in limbo since launching Unknown 9. Whatever existing property the developer was working on, the project clearly didn't make the cut.

We wish those impacted by the closure all the best for the future.

#4081. Wooshy wuxia actioner Phantom Blade Zero is sharp enough on the Steam Machine, if blunted on the Steam Deck

It would appear that Phantom Blade Zero (Phantom Blade 0? Zero? Let’s go with Zero) demanding more gigs than a mismanaged stadium is doing little to stop people playing the thing. It therefore stands to reason at least some folks will want to run S-Game Studio’s lightly Soulsy sword-em-up on the Steam Machine, so let us now examine how said GabeCube stands up to its effects-heavy martial artistry. With some settings proposals, natch.

Two signs boded poorly, before I got to testing the Machine. The first was a comment on Oisin’s day one patch piece, warning of heavy glitching on a Linux system. The second was my Steam Deck OLED, also a Linux system, being incapable of running Phantom Blade Zero at even close to a steady 30fps; even with the Low preset and some nasty-looking Ultra Performance upscaling, the game’s flashy moves and jerking (apologies – cinematic) camera shifts made for regular framerate drops into the teens.

Fortunately, the Steam Machine is much more resilient, even if it does benefit from a few quality cuts (and, realistically, will struggle if pushed beyond standard 1080p.) The Medium preset and Quality-level FSR are enough for 45-60fps in what I’ve played so far, and the High preset – while a touch susceptible to sub-40fps dips for my liking – is at least playable without major bugs or stuttering.

Strangely enough, the only major technical problem I’ve had wasn’t caused by graphics, or the Linux-based SteamOS, but the Steam Controller I was playing with. Despite being assured during the boot process that I was being treated to the Official Gamepad Configuration – cor! – an unresponsive map-opening button left me immobile during a prompt tutorial. Immobile and, I suppose without a map, lost. It turns out this this is a common bug with the Steam Controller specifically, and can be fixed by remapping the Select button, in SteamOS’s controller settings, to emulate the effect of clicking the touchpad of a PS5 pad. PC gaming.

With that sorted, Phantom Blade Zero seems to work fine? If I was nitpicking I’d point out that some high-drama sequences are visibly less buttery than the slower, roaming sections, which can exceed 60fps on Medium. Same for a lot of cutscenes, which aren’t hard-locked to 30fps like prerendered scenes often are, but do cause heavy framerate drops for little apparent reason. Still, it’s reasonable when actually playing.

Settings-wise, that Medium preset (with FSR on Quality) works well if you’re lazy. But a few of Phantom Blade Zero’s individual quality options aren’t terribly performance-sapping by themselves, and than thus be tuned upwards for a slightly nicer-looking wuxia tale with minimal drawback. Have a crack with the following:

Don’t miss those Dynamic Resolution Quality and Super Resolution Output Scale tweaks; on their defaults, they both make the game uglier than it needs to be. And on the subject of Super Resolution, FSR upscaling does leave a bit of roughness on certain edges, but then at 1080p, so does FSR even when it’s on its Native Resolution setting. You might as well get the extra frames.

#4080. PSA: Nintendo Ending Google And Apple Sign-Ins On Nintendo Accounts In 2027

You'll need a Nintendo Account from here on out

If you currently use a Google or Apple account to sign in to your Nintendo Account, Nintendo has got some news. In an official notice, it's announced the discontinuation of Google and Apple account sign-ins on Nintendo Accounts.

This will take place on 26th January 2027, so we're just a few months out. "As of" this date, it will no longer be possible to link a Google or Apple account. Nintendo notes this exact end time "may be delayed depending on the progress of the system change work".

Nintendo: "We apologise for any inconvenience to those who used a Google or Apple account to sign in to their Nintendo Account."

Here's what this means when it does come into effect:

And "if you are already logged into your Nintendo Account on a device, you may not have to sign in again". If the sign-in page does appear, you'll need to sign in using the email address or sign-in ID and your password for your Nintendo Account, or a Passkey.

If we hear any updates about this, we'll let you know. What are your thoughts about this announcement? Let us know in the comments.

#4079. Skyrim lead doubted Todd Howard’s constellation-based skill system, and then the RPG came out

Making games like Skyrim requires a lot of collaboration. Disagreement is inherent to such projects, and in one instance, a tenured Bethesda developer remembers not seeing Todd Howard's vision for character progression before players demonstrated it was the right course to take.

Bruce Nesmith, a designer who worked on Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim at Bethesda, explained the situation on The Examined Game podcast. "Todd had this vision for how the constellations would reflect your skills," he starts.

"He was looking at the art and wanted the art to drive some of how the skills related to one another," he continues. "I was like, 'No, you're going up you're looking at these, why can't we just put a list out, it's far more functional. People are going to get confused by these constellations, it's not going to work, I'm not seeing it.'"

Skyrim's skill trees being literally made up of stars in the night sky was a visual leap from the number sets of Oblivion. It's an eye-catching approach, and I remember it took me a second to get used to what I was seeing. But once I did, I enjoyed the added flair, and plenty of others did too, according to Nesmith, who wound up with a little egg on his face.

"I held that all the way through production, and the game gets out there, and people loved the constellations," he recalls. "They thought they were fantastic. I was clearly wrong."

He credits Howard with having both the better idea and the leadership position to take the risk on it. A foundational requirement of good collaboration is someone at the helm who can sense what the right direction is when there are split decisions, regardless of who comes up with it. This is one instance where Howard had the pleasure of being both.

We'll see what lays in store in The Elder Scrolls 6, and who'll take the blame for the problems. Howard seems like a good default candidate either way.

#4078. Warframe's fantasy-pilled sister Soulframe finally goes open to all this November, though Digital Extremes are "nervous" about certain changes

They're celebrating the end of closed alpha by poisoning the world

Warframe creators Digital Extremes have announced that their free-to-play fantasy RPG Soulframe will be available for everyone to download on 6th November, after two years in closed alpha. Finally, you serfs without "prelude" keys will be able to fire up Soulframe.com and make sense of my ranting about the sleeping animals on the lobby screen.

The new "open prelude" will land shortly before the game's 17th major update, Verse of the Veilands, which lets you grow your Omen wolfpup allies into rideable adult wolves by finding the ingredients for a special biscuit. More importantly, prelude 17 violently rearranges the game's wistful world, adding an Ubisoft-esque region purging system that is designed to guide new players a bit more emphatically towards the game's "votives". Aka, missions. Yes, Digital Extremes sort of have a bespoke term for every game feature in Soulframe. I find this can be either charming or maddening, depending on how much sleep I've had.

Here's how the region purging will work: after completing the game's Tormented Stag quest, you'll find that the landscape is being corrupted by siphons deployed by the villainous star-faring Ode faction. You have to complete votives to build energy and learn the sacred song of each region, allowing you to cleanse it and restore the environment.

In a roundtable preview session last week, creative director Geoff Crookes and lead designer Scott McGregor expressed a certain amount of anxiety about deliberately polluting Soulframe's fairytale ambience. "Scott and I were just talking yesterday about, aesthetically, how nervous we are about this change," Crookes commented, "because the game has gotten a lot of really great feedback on how cosy it is, how beautiful the world is, and you're going to enter a game that is much more unforgiving and harsh at first glance."

That said, he thinks the shift "pairs really well with going into open alpha, because it is a much stronger breadcrumb [trail] for the player, to pull them into the world and give them a bit more ownership of what they're doing." Once rinsed of Ode siphons, regions will appear more like how they are in previous versions of Soulframe, with activities such as fishing and new resources to snaffle.

McGregor added that hitherto, a lot of Soulframe players have gotten lost and put the game down after completing the opening "Fables", or story quests. "It's a really big change to the structural flow of the game, you know," he told the assembled journorabble. "We're very open and discoverable, and we had a lot of player feedback that was basically 'what do I do next? What do I do next? I don't know what to do next'.

"So [it's] taking that and mashing it with the votive system, which is our mission system for the game, and making that more of a directed experience," he went on, "and then once they get through that directed experience, they can go back to that open world." Prelude 17 will also let you accept votives more straightforwardly from the world map, after finding the local representative or mission giver.

Digital Extremes have a new Soulframe "pact" or character loadout on the boil, the Ode Shrike. It's a dastardly poacher class who specialises in spike traps and throwable bolas. The Shrike's standout ability is a balloon dart that lets you hoist enemies into the sky, as in Metal Gear Solid V.

You can read more about Soulframe's on-going reinventions on the official site. While you won't need a key to get access as of Nov 6th, the game's paid Founders program will remain the same. Digital Extremes will likely still run closed preview builds alongside the "open prelude", testing out features with a smaller group of players. They're also looking into giving you the ability to reset your character, so you can check out any new material added to parts of the game you've finished.

I'm not sure I've ever been exhilarated by Soulframe, but I like the poise, flamboyance and gentle complexity of its combat. I also really enjoy its faded tapestry aesthetics, though I think it's yanking on the goo-goo glands too avidly with all these fluffy forest animals. Enough photogenic wolfpups, Digital Extremes - let's see you make, I don't know, a blobfish look adorable.

It's also very interesting as a new live service project from a company defined by the success of Warframe. I spoke to the Soulframe developers earlier in the year about the challenge of borrowing Warframe's thunder without getting lost in its shadow.

#4077. Feature: These Are Xbox's Best 25 Games From 2001-2026 According To Metacritic

As we continue our celebrations for Xbox's 25th anniversary this Sunday (November 15th), we thought it might be fun to look back at the past 25 years on Metacritic, and specifically the best-rated Xbox games from each year.

The website has a significant history of review roundups dating all the way back to 2001, and looking at the list, the early years in particular are jam-packed with historic Xbox games! Halo is in there multiple times, as is Gears of War and Grand Theft Auto, and then we start to see an indie explosion with the likes of Inside and Hades in later years.

So, here are Xbox's best 25 games from 2001-2026 according to Metacritic from each individual year. Just keep in mind that we've eliminated a couple of expansions, as we're only counting full game releases.

Of course, when it comes to 2026 specifically, there's every chance GTA 6 will end up taking the top spot within a couple of weeks' time, so just keep that in mind - Hades 2 has done amazingly well, but will most likely be surpassed.

And by the way, this list doesn't tell the full story - here's what it would look like if you took the individual years away:

Pretty different, right? It's no surprise that there were multiple years that fared better than others in terms of highly-rated releases, so the likes of The Orange Box, Red Dead Redemption 2, Portal 2, Halo 3 and others still make the lineup.

Anyway, Metacritic doesn't tell the full story by any means here, but it's a useful resource to look back and see how well the critics positioned these games at the time, and whether we reckon they're still justifying their high scores.

So, what do you reckon to these? We'd love to hear your thoughts down in the comments section below.

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

There is undoubtedly a time when review scores became more inline with the scores we see today. In other words, there is no way that Halo: Combat Evolved would score 97 under todays review score regime. Don't misunderstand me, Halo: CE is still a great game, but if reviewed today it would be marked down for its samey locations, limited enemy types etc. etc. (and I just picked that game, rather than picking on that game).

I wonder when that would have been? Any thoughts, @FraserG?

Does the passing of each generation further refine the scores that professional reviewers give, and I wonder what those same games would be given if reviewed today...?

I don't think there's any guarantee that gta6 gets a higher average review than 95, so Hades 2 may well end the year with top spot.

@Fiendish-Beaver I think about this a lot. Really, only Nintendo games can break the 95 barrier now.

@Llamageddon Yeah, 95 is a tough score to beat. It could be tight for R* to contend with that.

@Fiendish-Beaver I agree with the Halo point. I think a lot of games back then got a lot of praise due to the graphical jumps between generations. I mean, 16bit > 32bit was ridiculously jaw-dropping. The same can be said about 64bit > 128bit. I think many games from the Xbox / PS2 / Gamecube era wowed more than impressed. We don't really see that today, do we? Generational jumps just seem so slight (when we compare games at the end of one gen to the beginning of the next). That said, Halo 4 is the best Halo for me, followed by 1, then 2, then ODST. Halo 3 can go kick rocks. That game sucked.

Hey, @Kaloudz. Nice to see you around. Hope you are well, matey.

I agree, it was probably the wow factor that saw games receive such high scores back when gaming was much younger, and I suspect that by early in the Xbox One / PS3 era (so probably 2015ish) we had experienced much of what there was to see, and so we moved from wow to technicality. We started to judge games more on performance and variety, their technical achievement and overall enjoyment. I'd say we don't judge games based on their graphical prowess because otherwise all these retro style games would be marked down severely, which obviously does not happen.

Gains in consoles are so incremental these days that I think a game that released from 2015 onwards is probably judged by much the same standards now as it was back then.

What would be interesting, would be for someone to take up reviewing games, and to review older games but by todays standards. So someone that had never played the first Gears of War, plays it through, and gives it a review score based not on the wow, but on its technical achievements, level design, enemy variety, and what have you. I imagine that we would see a very different set of scores if games were reviewed now from what they were given when they originally released, but it would be interesting to see just how these older games would fair...

@Fiendish-Beaver I agree it is harder to get to that 95ish score than it was. I think there's a few different things going on there.

Firstly as @Kaloudz said there was a big graphical jump between generations. But there was also much larger GAMEPLAY jumps back then too. Games and their mechanics were often breaking new paradigms whether that was Mario or Zelda in 3D for the first time or Gears and Halo pushing third and third person console shooters into the mainstream on console. It felt exciting. Now most games feel much more iterative, especially AAA games.

There were also typically fewer reviews for each game, and those reviews were generally from a smaller cross-section of gamers in similar demographics who were more likely to have similar tastes, that led to homogenisation of some scores. Now a game might be marked down by a new demographic, which is fair enough, aggregate scores don't tell the whole story, we all like different things.

Linked to that I know some people believe that Nintendo games get unfairly scored higher than they might for some reason, but I don't see it that way. I think there is often a universal joy to Nintendo games that resonates with far more players. More simply put: they haven't forgotten how to make their games joyful and fun on an almost primal level. That won't be for everyone - nothing is - but it is for a wider cross section of people, and reviewers, hence they are more likely to score higher as an aggregate.

Look at Ocarina of Time remake. Not only a hit with critics currently scoring 96 on Metacritic from 94 reviews but also currently a 9.6 from 10.5k user reviews, it's rare to see both critics and users in such harmony. Having swallowed it whole and finished it already, I would agree it's the easiest 10 in years imho. Bring on GTA6.

As for the list as you'd expect with a best of list it's wall to wall bangers. I'm surprised there's more games than I thought on that list I haven't played yet, but I really struggle to start 100+ hour games like Persona 5 or BG3. One day!

@Fiendish-Beaver Oh i'll get to it. I have no doubt, and it's not through lack of interest either. I just struggle to start games that I know will take me 100+ hours... and this one probably 200+ hours. (FYI your 1000 hours isn't helping!!! lol)

I love self employment, flexibility of work hours, but when I REALLY get into a game I often make poor life choices, and work or life suffers with no one looking over my shoulder. That is fine for something like Ocarina of Time remake - book Thursday and Friday off and finish it across 4 days, it's not that long and doesn't really impact my life.

But for games like Elden Ring, BG3, CyberPunk etc. that I pretty much KNOW I will fall head over heels into and at least partially no-life for weeks I need to be very careful when I start them. Pretty much all my most want to play games fall into this group sadly. I have at least twenty 100+ hour games near the top of my backlog.

Yes, sorry, @themightyant. I do occasionally forget that people do not have the luxury of time that I enjoy these days. If I want to game 8 hours a day every day for a fortnight that is something I could easily do (I don't, but I could).

It is a big time commitment, of that there is no doubt, and I totally understand what you mean when you say you find it off-putting because that is precisely why I have not played Assassin's Creed: Valhalla, and why I may not end up playing Crimson Desert, both of which I own, but neither of which I have played. I'd like to play them, but in the case of Valhalla, I worry I will get bored towards the end, which is what happened with both Odyssey and Origins, both of which I never finished despite putting over 100 into each of them. In the case of Crimson Desert, it feels like they keep adding to the game, and so I don't know when to start it because I will probably only want to play it once, but also want it to be feature complete by which time it will probably be to daunting to start.

If it helps, I think my 1000 hours in BG3 is divided over 4 different runs in the game. It is probably possible to complete it in under 200 hours, and that should enable you to see everything outside different story choices. According to howlongtobeat.com BG3 should take you around 180 hours if you do both mains and sides, though different choices can change the game pretty drastically...

@Fiendish-Beaver Strangely I have less concerns over something like AC: Valhalla because although it's long I know I would get a bit bored and can put it down. It's unlikely to grip me in the same way.

The problem is games I fall completely in love with and I end up staying up till the birds are tweeting, or trying to fit a few hours play into the work day.

For me it's Elden Ring, BG3, Cyberpunk, FF7 Rebirth, Persona, KCD, Hades, Monster Hunter, Death Stranding, MGSV, Metaphor re:F, Xenoblades... plenty of lengthy RPGs in fact. The platinum does extend it quite considerably though and can be a bit of a grind (if you're an achievement hunter). I would also thoroughly recommend the game (one of my personal all time favourites).

@AlwaysPlaying also giving gta6 an 8 out of 10 (when most are giving it 10s) would drive a lot of traffic to that review even if it was pure rage baiting. I like to think all reviewers have the integrity to not do that but I'm not naive enough to believe that's the case.

One of my favourite memories in gaming is playing Horde in Gears 3 with 4 of my mates, with the game finally ending at 4 a.m., and whilst I know that is not particularly late (in terms of what we are talking about) the host had to be up at 5 a.m. in order to go to work! We still wax lyrical about that to this day, and that was well over 10 years ago now.

@themightyant absolutely, supergiant is one of my favourite small Devs, great consistency and variety. Look forward to what they cook up next (as much as I love the Hades games, they have too much talent to be stuck making one series).

#4076. Marathon's Fate Hangs in the Balance as Bungie Details Its Game-Saving PvE Update

Bungie has reconfirmed that Marathon's major 'Symbiosis' update will launch on the 8th December. You may recall that it was delayed back in September.

Many believe that this patch will be the troubled shooter's make-or-break moment, as Marathon's player numbers remain concerningly low.

The good news is that Symbiosis looks the part. A new trailer highlights its additions, which include a brand new PvE mode titled Expedition.

The official description reads: "Phase 1 of a new PvE-only mode built around a three-run series. Play solo or with a crew, face new combat and environmental challenges without PvP threats, and use Flash Boosts to shape your build during a run."

Basically, Bungie's hoping that the introduction of a non-competitive option draws in new players — and I suppose that's a logical avenue to go down, given that Marathon's struggled to crack the extraction shooter market.

The update also packs a new team-based 'Deathmatch' mode in its beta form, a new social space called Limbo, and a new Runner Shell (character class) named Bishop. A couple of new weapons are up for grabs, too.

And last but certainly not least, Marathon's going free-to-play for a full week when the Symbiosis update drops. Worth a shot?

Do you still play Marathon? Might you be going back for this big update? Check those corners in the comments section below.

#4075. What are we all playing this weekend?

My scares should have been reserved for today, what with it being All Hallows' Eve and all, but my fright came on Thursday.

It was a dark October night and I was returning from work. A storm had blown through earlier in the week, so the evening was unusually crisp and clear. I walked between the terrace houses, feeling the eyes of work-from-homers on my back. I turned the key in the door to the communal hallway, climbed the creaky stairs, and tried to keep my footsteps light as I passed my rude neighbour's flat. My head was wholly absorbed by the prospect of the risotto I had waiting in the fridge/

I unlocked my front door and started up the internal staircase to the kitchen, not even bothering to turn on the lights. Out of the dark, something jumped down the stairs at me, hitting me in the stomach. I flicked the lights on in a panic and saw a small brown thing with a long tail bolting back up the staircase. A mouse. In my house.

Terrifying stuff, I'm sure you will agree. It almost put me off my risotto. Anyway, this is what the rest of the team will be up to this weekend..

OllieI've settled into a very comfy rhythm of playing the latest Trackmania campaign and also a bit of Factorio, both with my brother. When I've a bit of time to myself I'm also interested in trying out Queen's Domain. Heard good things!

JeremyI continue to chip away at our Castlevania walkthrough as it chips away at my soul. Such is the transactional bargain of dealing with Dracula during Halloween, no? However, as I answer the door for trick-or-treaters, I may partake in what is becoming an annual tradition - watching an old game playthrough on YouTube as I hand out sweets. I'm thinking I will watch the 1994 SNES game Nosferatu this year, which is not related to Castlevania but does feature a bold guy going to beat up Dracula and all of his minions with nothing but his feet and fists.

JamesMy previously mentioned attempts to play Mortal Shell 2 have been thwarted this week by, in chronological order, work, social obligations, brownie making, Deep Rock Galactic, and more brownie making. We go again.

EdwinI'm helping with a house move this weekend, so I doubt I'll have much time for your foolish computer entertainments, but I'd like to crack on with Queen's Domain and also, try out Danchi Days, a sorrowful comedy about trying to revive a summer festival in a 2000s-era Japanese neighbourhood.

CallumSuspiciously, Callum has been making squeaking noises in meetings. Is this a sign he planted the mouse? Perhaps he was the mouse. Surely, it's not a coincidence. There's no such thing as coincidence when it comes to mice.

MarkI want to finish Virtue and a Sledgehammer, having started it the other night. I really dug The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood, one of Spanish studio Deconstructeam's previous games. Thus far, VaaS is hitting just as hard in terms of emotional beats, but in a manner that's more haunting than charming. We'll see where I land on it by the end.

JulianAs well as searching my flat for mouse hidey holes, I will be (touch wood/cross fingers/make a sacrifice to Bob the Builder) finishing the DIY I started last weekend. Alcove bookcases and a painted living room are in my future, I just have to manifest it.

Besides that, I've been dipping my toes into Titanium Court. I like it but I don't so far love it. It's witty, the presentation is excellent, but I feel like it is also keeping me at arm's length and I want to be drawn into its world, not kept at a distance. It may just need more time. I will also be trying hard not to sweep the moon.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

#4074. Unknown 'Mega Man Legends' Project Surfaces Online

As Capcom gears up for Mega Man's 40th anniversary next year, more findings related to the long-running IP are surfacing online.

As reported by Mega Man fan site Rockman Corner, a production titled 'Mega Man Legends' has appeared on ACTRA Toronto's "What's Shooting" database (a public listing of production registered with the Canadian performers' union) this week.

It's filed under "new media" and the production start date was in September, with it scheduled to wrap up by December. Casting is apparently in house, but that's all that's known about the mysterious project.

As the source notes, "new media" could be everything from "video games to television and film". It's also mentions how Capcom "could be looking to Canadian voice talent as an alternative to SAG-AFRA Actors" after "Mega Man: Dual Override became the subject of a SAG-AFTRA 'Do Not Work' order" earlier this year.

Mega Man Legends was originally released as a 3D video game in 1997 and was followed by a second game in 2000. There was also a prequel spin-off in 1999, and a cancelled third entry for the 3DS.

This latest finding also follows a rating board classification in Korea at the end of last month. It featured various classic Capcom console titles, including multiple Mega Man games.

News Multiple Capcom Console Classics Have Been Rated In Korea

If we hear anything else about this listing, we'll provide an update.

Analysts report it's already beaten Cyberpunk 2077's pre-order record of 8 million copies

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, GTA 6 is reportedly the most pre-ordered game of all time, with Sony and Microsoft confirming that's at least the case for the PlayStation Store and Xbox Store.

Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower has reported via its sales tracker that GTA 6 has sold an estimated 9.69 million copies through pre-orders ahead of the game's launch next week. Per its data, GTA 6 has already made just shy of a billion with $942 million in revenue. Unsurprisingly, given its larger install base and co-marketing deal, PlayStation is leading, with roughly 75% of pre-orders (7.23 million copies) on PS5, while Xbox has roughly 25% (2.46 million copies), per the data provided. This beats Cyberpunk 2077 as the most pre-ordered game, with CD Projekt Red announcing over 8 million pre-orders ahead of its disastrous launch.

Following Sensor Tower's data release, Sony posted on the PlayStation Blog to celebrate the availability of GTA 6 preloads. In this post, Sony confirms that "Grand Theft Auto 6 is now the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store." Shortly after, Microsoft published a post on Xbox Wire, calling GTA 6 "the most pre-ordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store."

Frankly, I'd have been shocked if GTA 6 wasn't the most pre-ordered game of all time. As much as it pales in comparison to my personal pre-release hype for Donkey Kong Bananza, there's never been a game with a fever quite like this – I mean, when has a game ever had a music festival dedicated to it? If anything, I'm shocked it didn't become that right away after 13 years of waiting.
