#4072. Horror-steeped card game Forbidden Solitaire shows how a strong theme can elevate even decade-old mechanics

Like a tag team of oiled snakes that have entered a wrestling contest, theme is a difficult quality to pin down. A game can be well designed, but if it lacks a coherence between those mechanics and its appearance, narrative, and its framing, there is a dissonance that can be hard to ignore. I realise I've just stepped into an old argument by using the word 'dissonance', but Hocking was right, games that don't cohere can be jarring. A developer may desire that sensation of discomfort, but often it is accidental and unwanted.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

(Much like opening an article with a simile about wrestling snakes when there is nothing connecting that image to a game about solitaire. It might be a good line, but it doesn't smoothly connect with the rest of the article to elevate its argument.)

Anyway, what does this all have to do with Forbidden Solitaire, a game in which you're delving deeper into a dungeon filled with horrors, progressing by clearing screens of cards? Well, it's an excellent example of how well-handled theming can raise a game into something more than its parts.

I've been playing Grey Alien Games' work since they released Regency Solitaire in 2015, and their games often revolve around the same core, Solitaire-inspired mechanics. Each level is a screen filled with stacks of playing cards, and you must clear the screen by picking cards that are one higher or lower than the one currently in your hand. In addition to standard playing cards, you may find padlock cards which can only be cleared with a matching key card, special cards that reshuffle all the stacks, or ones that change cards into suits or numbers that may help you. Except, in each of their games – Regency Solitaire, Shadowhand, Ancient Enemy, and now Forbidden Solitaire - the scenario for those mechanics changes, and in doing do, they show the power of recontextualising.

In Forbidden Solitaire, you're playing a game within a game. Although it's set in 2019, your character is playing a 1995 CD-ROM they found in a second-hand shop. It's one you vaguely remember from your childhood, if mainly for the controversy it caused at launch. The game sees you breaking into an old dungeon and exploring its depths. Each locked door that blocks you, labyrinth that puzzles you, or enemy that challenges you is tackled with the mechanics of Grey Alien Games' previous releases: screens of stacked cards to be cleared. Even familiar special cards, such as the one which shuffles all the cards before you, make a return. As you progress through Forbidden Solitaire's dungeon, you're interrupted by messages from your sister in the present, who is researching the game and the controversy surrounding it, sending you links to police reports, old news clips of the secretive developer, and hidden documents on a centuries-old group of cultists.

Yet, despite the mechanical familiarity, it's this fresh theme that elevates Forbidden Solitaire into something special. For new players, the 1995 game framing device immediately gives an allowance for the simple card mechanics, and allows them to sink into the kitsch horror story of cult members developing haunted video games. But, for returning players like me, I can see all the neat ways the old tools have been adapted to fit this new world. When you find a person marked for sacrifice tied to a bed, for instance, the level to free them is filled with locks that only disappear when you match enough cards of the same suit. It's a pairing of unlocking mechanics that have been in Grey Alien Games' work for at least the past decade to a moment in the story where you are untying a character. The action dovetails with the narrative perfectly.

Anyway, when I realised the role that theme had to play in Forbidden Solitaire, I was feeling extremely smart and smug. Then I reread Adam (RPS in peace) and Pip's (RPS in peace) Regency Solitaire verdict from 2015.

Adam: I think the whole game is a superb example of how a decent design can be elevated by a strong theme. It’s not even particularly overindulgent - flourishes throughout but no extended dialogues or huge slabs of exposition. It’s a few attractive backgrounds (though with an inaccurate non-pebbled Brighton beach, I’m told by RPS chatroom stalwart and Brighton denizen Alec Meer), a handful of characters and miniature conversations to set the tone. But it’s all done so well. It seems to be aware of its own posture in a way that allows it to be well-mannered, well-meaning and not at all over-bearing.

If it had been pixies or space marines, I don’t think I’d have been particularly interested at all - and that’s not to say the actual card game isn’t well-constructed because it is - but even though the story is slight, it’s a great reward at the end of a few hands.

Pip: I'd agree with that, particularly about the setting. It's a game that has a good understanding of its own size, scope and the tone which suits it.

Those absolute cads. Still, go play Forbidden Solitaire anyway. It's a far better time than trying to get an oiled snake into a three-piece suit.

#4071. Beloved Co-Op Adventure Big Walk in Hot Water After Failing to Disclose AI Usage

Big Walk, one of the most highly-rated games of 2026, has suddenly found itself in a spot of bother, and it's all thanks to those controversial AI tools.

This story stems from the Independent Games Festival Awards (IGF); some of the jurors have taken a hard stance against usage of generative AI or LLM technology.

These jurors recently put out a statement in which they condemn the tech, and in the aftermath of this, it's come out that developer House House did in fact use gen AI, albeit in a minor capacity, when making Big Walk.

On the game's official website, this is now addressed directly in a new FAQ page.

In the statement, House House says LLMs were used "sparingly" near the end of the game's production "to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs."

"In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

The statement goes on to provide an example of how and why the tech was used.

Ultimately, it seems the team has utilised AI very minimally, but that its use was not previously disclosed has rubbed people the wrong way.

Usually, generative AI usage is declared on a game's Steam page, but House House says it didn't do so because "the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage" but has made it public information in light of IGF's actions.

It opens up the debate about gen AI once again. Whether you like it or not, more and more games are being built with the tech to varying degrees, and I expect the number will only grow bigger over time.

However, its ubiquity doesn't safeguard it from criticism, especially when it comes to generating in-game assets, writing, or other creative aspects.

In Big Walk's case, an LLM was used to help with specific technical issues, which I think is relatively harmless, but others may still feel any gen AI is too much.

We either need to be much clearer about how it is specifically used, which will get harder and more and more tools use it by default, or drop the tag altogether. It's currently not fit for purpose.

@nessisonett Technically, "gen AI" describes AI systems capable of producing new content based on patterns learned during training. That content can take many forms:

What you call (modern) "AI assisted debugging" is as "gen AI" as generating art assets. The underlying technology may differ (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), but most AI models these days are multimodal in nature, combining multiple technologies to achieve the desired results.

You could refine that distinction and say you're against using AI to generate content trained on protected IP. But even then, you'd be in muddy waters somewhat, because source code is as copyrighted as art.

#4070. NACON Releases REVO Range Of Xbox Controllers Designed For 'Every Gamer Style'

"Always Ready. Tailored Control. Pros' Arsenal."

NACON has announced today the availability of its REVO range of Xbox controllers, three officially licensed pads. The trio aims to accommodate the needs of every Xbox and PC player, because "every gamer has a style, every style has a controller."

The REVO X and REVO X MAX are available for purchase today, with the REVO X PRO arriving sometime in 2027. All three controllers are designed for different player styles, and so we've listed the price point and details for each pad. Here's how NACON described the REVO range:

"The new range has been designed to meet the specific needs of every type of player, from the casual gamer looking for the immediate efficiency of a "Plug-and-Play" controller, to the esports expert seeking deep customization."

The REVO controller is the embodiment of accessible and reliable performance. It is ideal for players looking for fluid control and flawless durability.

Announced for 2027, the REVO PRO is designed for the most demanding competitive players. It combines the best features of the range, including instant micro-switch triggers and programmable rear buttons, to offer optimized responsiveness and control for competition.

For players who demand complete customization, the REVO MAX offers advanced adjustment options to adapt the controller to their playstyle; these options are in addition to all the REVO features detailed above.

If you fancy picking up the REVO X or REVO X MAX, you can head to NACON's store directly via this link, or by the links embedded in each title above.

#4069. The Sunday Papers

Sundays are for looking upon my DIY works and despairing. Strewn sawdust, spilled paint, and hunks of broken MDF litter my living room kingdom. When will it be over? When will I be free? When will I be able to reassemble my sofa, sit down with a cup of tea in hand, and admire my books, unpacked and arranged on perfectly fitted alcove bookshelves?

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

"Today?" I whisper hopefully in response to a paragraph of rhetorical questions. "Probably not," snaps back Reality. Especially if I don't get out of bed soon. Still, here in bed I can read the best writing about and not about games from the past week.

Inside our Gchat walls, there is a growing exhaustion with genAI stories. Every day another gaming boss talks about the inexorable march of the tech before putting out a trailer filled with blurry text and six-fingered characters. I don't doubt the tech is getting better, but it's not inevitable. As such, Rob Fahey's latest GI column is something of a balm:

There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.

At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.

A further tonic comes from Merritt K, who writes for Aftermath about the technological improvements rolling through Karaoke.

Doesn't it feel like everything — especially everything Big Tech touches — is getting worse? Generative AI, not merely content with robbing humans of our craft and jobs, has escaped containment into physical reality in the form of shitty event flyers and small business signage. Hugely profitable industries like video games and film are being torn apart by the financialization of the economy as shareholders seek ever-increasing short-term profits. Algorithmic pricing of rent and groceries threatens to further punish the working class for the crime of not being born rich.

But in the heart of despair, we must reach for that which is good and pure and — dare I say it — better than it used to be. Karaoke is one of those things. And it is better not because of the disruption of tech giants, but, as is often the case, thanks to the work of enterprising maniacs toiling in obscurity, purely out of the love of the game.

I've been playing Forbidden Solitaire this week, where FMV sequences starring Xalavier Nelson Jr as an obsessive fantasy-author-turned-video-game-developer are played for laughs. So it was with a minor sense of whiplash I read Ashley Bardhan's piece for This Week In Video Games. Bardhan speaks to horror developers inserting themselves into FMV games to confront and explore violence against women.

Cara Cadaver uses her own photos and videos to represent multiple victims of sexual violence and murder in her unflinching 2025 game Vile: Exhumed. She tells me over email, “Being a woman is inherently a horrifying and violent experience, any way you slice it. One of my inspirations for making games in general is pulling from real-life experience and telling stories that most every woman has lived in some way; that’s real horror.”

“Horror in general has been a major outlet for me while dealing with trauma, and so much of horror as a genre goes back to women,” Cadaver says. “Women’s stories belong in horror — and that has been the case as long as horror has existed.”

Over at RPS-but-it's-The-Fade, Brendan's run through what made Bioware games great (and also terrible).

Bioware established romance as a must for any blockbuster RPG worth its frost salts (and not just RPGs).

Kissing your friends on the mouth is everywhere in mainstream and indie games today. It's a verb now. Characters are "romanceable". I played Nivalis Nights last month and could not get away from the swarms of horny NPC citizens trying to jump my noodle serving bones. Baldur's Gate 3 launched with a bug that made your companions fuckable in just a few nights, and people didn't even notice. They thought: that's normal and right, I should shag everyone, gender and orientation be damned. See that mountain? You can fuck it. And that's (at least partially) thanks to Bioware.

GTA is an unignorable thing. It is one of those breakout cultural objects that has its own gravity, drawing in attention and comment from politicians, mainstream press, parents, schools, comedians, columnists, footballers, taxi drivers, and hairdressers. In all the weight of it, I hadn't yet really seen it as a game. Simon Parkin's Edge cover feature may not reveal many new details about the game but it has made me appreciate it as a game (and maybe even get a little bit excited for its eventual PC release.

Nelson, grave-faced but friendly, wearing all black, with grey-flecked stubble, settles into a leather-and-chrome Eames chair while we perch on a burnt-orange sofa facing a pair of expansive wall-mounted TVs. In the past, Rockstar has carefully stage-managed encounters such as this. For previews of previous GTAs, one team member played the game while a publicist read from a pre-prepared script, further evidence of the paranoia that can take hold when an artist is working on something the entire world is desperate to see.

Today, however, Nelson has no script and, apparently, no plan. For the next 90 minutes he simply plays the current build, following his nose, confident that the game's systems will hold together wherever he pushes them, that this world's glories will glint and shimmer no matter which angle he approaches from. It is an extraordinary demonstration not of paranoia but of trust – in the game, in the team that built it, perhaps even in us.

Nelson picks up the controller and lets Grand Theft Auto VI speak for itself.

I am guilty of forgetting and looking away, but the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has not ended, it is deepening. Writing for the LRB, Selma Dabbagh bluntly captures the ugly events of the past two years :

In January 2025 Donald Trump described Gaza as a ‘demolition site’. ‘You’re talking about probably a million and a half people,’ he said, ‘and we just clean out that whole thing.’ The number is closer to two million people – not a ‘whole thing’ but two million individual human beings – who have been driven into an area that’s less than a third of the densely inhabited land they lived on. Their cities and arable lands – palms, olives, coriander, citrus and pomegranate trees – have been obliterated.

I'd like there to be a big reason for this week's music recommendation, but really it's just a little victory lap. I managed to nab some tickets to see This Is The Kit, so give Bashed Out a listen, yeah?

#4068. Skydance boss says AI could become "the biggest creative unlock in modern history"

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

Bringing all the latest movie news, features, and reviews to your inbox

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Skydance boss David Ellison has spoken out about AI use in projects, not long after James Gunn and Peter Safran departed as heads of DC Studios.

“I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history," Ellison said on Skydance's latest earnings call (via The Verge).

Ellison then compared the breakthrough – if you want to call it that – to the emergence of CGI and special effects in the 1990s, name-checking both Jurassic Park and Terminator 2 as beneficiaries of that leap in technology.

Ellison continued, "It's hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.”

While Ellison, who now heads up Skydance after the acquisition of Paramount and Warner Bros., may be waxing lyrical about AI usage, he does warn that artists remain key to his vision.

“In a world of AI slop, we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling," Ellison said. "We also continue to believe that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists and will never be a replacement for them."

It's unclear exactly how or to what extent AI will be used in upcoming Skydance projects – if at all – but it all comes off the back of a shocking DC shakeup as Jeremy Latcham was brought in to replace the outgoing Gunn and Safran

Later reports from The Wrap indicate that Ellison had been discussing Latcham taking over DC Studios as early as a month ago, prior to the Warner Bros. and Paramount merger as Skydance.

Upon their departure, Ellison said in a statement, "James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of. We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."

For more, we have a renewed look at the upcoming DC movies in the works, as well as all the movie release dates you need to know about as 2027 approaches.

#4067. Round Up: The Reviews Are In For Pikmin 4 - Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy

Following the anticipated return of Zelda: Ocarina of Time last week, Nintendo has now released Pikmin 4 - Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy. The critic reviews have now gone live. If you haven't already seen ours, we gave it seven stars, calling it a pleasant but perplexing piecemeal.

"Overall, £8/$10 is a small price to pay for some minor new features and a fun little mode that'll keep me entertained over the coming year, but it's more of a budding shoot right now than the full-bloom upgrade."

Mini Review Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy (Switch 2) - Pleasant But Perplexingly Piecemeal

And here's what other critics had to say:

"For late-bloomers who have yet to experience the magic that is Pikmin 4, the Nintendo Switch 2 Edition is the best place to start. Not only is native 4K resolution a significant improvement that allows the colourful world of Pikmin to shine brighter than ever before, Dandori Academy brings some worthwhile new content, held back only by Nintendo’s puzzling monthly stage distribution method. While not quite as extravagant as some of the other Nintendo Switch 2 Editions we’ve seen in recent memory, the lower-end $10 for the Upgrade Pack is an appropriate price point for what Pikmin 4 has to offer on Nintendo Switch 2; with the base game being in a class of its own."

"The main takeaway is that Pikmin 4 is still excellent, and I was grateful to transfer my save file from the Switch version (and I was tempted to start a new game + save), but Dandori Academy is not a strong incentive to return if you already played the game. It is a nice bonus and an interesting concept that reimagines the familiar time trial mode featured in plenty of video games, but the original campaign is still the main attraction."

"Pikmin 4 still remains one of my favourite titles released on the original Nintendo Switch, but unfortunately this update has left me feeling more than a little underwhelmed. While the game has seen a visual upgrade and the Oatchi commands are certainly a novel addition, the drip-feeding of its major new Dandori Academy content proves more frustrating than anything. More Pikmin is never a bad thing, but having to wait months to see it all, well… that’s a drag."

"Pikmin 4 is already a great time; Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy is just the 4K cherry on top. If you don’t own the original Switch version, then this is an easy recommendation; if you’re here for the upgrade/additions, then the visual upgrade will help. Dandori Academy won’t be for everyone, but over the next year it will continue to add extra challenges. The cheaper upgrade price point helps make it an easier recommendation."

PSA 'Pikmin 4 + Dandori Academy' Demo Blooms On Switch 2 Today

In this genAI world, every single leak that makes its way out into the world should be seen as more of a "leak" until proven otherwise. With that said, it does kind of seem like a remake of the first Persona game is on the way, with some footage supposedly leaking and showing it in action.

The leaked footage was shared yesterday to the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit, originally uploaded to the file-sharing site Gofile on Halloween, i.e. yesterday, i.e. October 31st. You will not at all be surprised to hear that, stylistically, it's incredibly in line with the vibe of contemporary Persona, a la the visual design established with Persona 5 that's been carried through to the Persona 3 and 4 remakes.

There's not a whole lot of footage to actually look at, just shy of two minutes all told. One bit shows the game's protagonist walking through a school at night before starting a battle. Again, the battle system looks like what you'd expect from Persona, being turn based and whatnot. The colour theme for this one is overwhelmingly purple, too, which at least lines up with the series' 25th anniversary artwork. What's perhaps slightly odd is that Persona 2's protagonist can be seen in battle; not sure if this is implying a combination of the two games, if two remakes are being made in tandem and it's a temporary use of assets, or if it's just an odd placeholder.

Persona 1 and 2 remakes wouldn't exactly be much of a surprise. Ashley interviewed series producer Kazuhisa Wada not too long ago, and he literally said "Persona 1 and 2 are something we’ll probably eventually do too." A knowing tease from Wada, perhaps? Who knows! Either way, the gameplay on display here looks believable, and Sega's leakier than a broken faucet (various Persona bits have leaked in the past too), so, something to keep an eye on at the very least, even if best taken with a pinch of salt.

A new billboard for Avengers: Doomsday might have spoiled a major detail about Thor's powers in the movie.

On the billboard, which you can see below, Thor is shown wielding yellow lightning. Usually, his lightning powers are a distinctive blue, which can be seen around Mjolnir on the billboard, which Steve Rogers is wielding.

New banners for ‘AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY’ have been spotted in Shanghai. https://t.co/iCOsrgdumJNovember 10, 2026

But, some Marvel fans think the billboard means Thor is going to be using the Odinforce in the film. Odinforce is yellow, and it's an extremely powerful ability that would make Thor pretty much unstoppable, if he truly is wielding it. But, it comes with a caveat: if it gets used too much, it triggers the Odinsleep. So, here's hoping Thor doesn't end up needing a nap on the battlefield.

"I just don't get why they'd put a massive spoiler for Thor," says one fan on Twitter, with another saying: "Odin force right in my face lmao"

However, considering it's featured on a billboard, it's unlikely that the Odinforce would be a dramatic reveal in the movie. Trailers so far have only shown Thor using his traditional blue lightning – but the yellow lightning has also featured as part of an action figure and on a poster, though it seemed to fly under the radar then.

#4064. Final Fantasy 14: Evercold sets itself a release date at the tail end of winter, alongside offering a look at its second, avian-inclined new job

Let's start with the bad news: Final Fantasy 14: Evercold has been delayed. The good news, that doesn't matter all that much, as it's only a delay of roughly a month, and a release date has been set in stone too: February 23rd, 2027. It's cutting it a bit close to the seasons shifting towards spring, making the game seasonally inappropriate, but hey ho, February is still winter!

That release date was revealed during this week's Final Fantasy 14 Fest Fest held in Tokyo. It was paired with a big ole cinematic that'll open up the expansion when you do actually get to play it. You can watch that down below if you fancy, that'll just depend on whether you want to go into the expansion knowing as little as possible. Looks pretty at least! I like the big dragony ship we've seen previously.

The expansion's second new job has been revealed too. It's called Zephyr, a physical ranged DPS that uses a crossbow and comes with its own avian familiar to assist you in battle. Seems like a pretty good option for folks afraid of getting in close but want to get some damage in. The bird friend you get is neat too. I hereby request that every other job gets a bird friend! I don't care if it doesn't make sense!

Most annoyingly, for me personally as someone that's only managed to play A Realm Reborn and doesn't really have time to go through a ridiculous number of hours and expansions just to get to this one, a preview for the Evangelion collab alliance raid was shown off rendered in the style of the original anime's post-credits, next episode teaser reels. I love those dang big robots and feelings of depression, don't make me go through all those expansions just to let my Viera dress up as Asuka or whatever loot you end up getting.

Anyway, don't forget to mark your calendars, February 23rd! Be there or be, uh, anywhere else I guess. I'm not your boss.

#4063. Here's What Xbox Owners Need To Know About 'Moving To New Zealand' For GTA 6

So, it's finally almost time for GTA 6. You've probably preloaded the game on your Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S already, and now you're eagerly awaiting the official launch that takes place on November 19th.

However, there are more than a few whispers going around about the "New Zealand" trick — something we've seen time and time again over the past decade-plus on Xbox — and it looks set to have a big influence again with GTA 6.

But what is it, and most importantly could it get you banned? Let's take a look at the facts:

On this page: Here's What Xbox Owners Need To Know About 'Moving To New Zealand' For GTA 6

A game like GTA 6 obviously has a set release date of November 19th, but it lands at "midnight local time" depending on the region you're in. That means New Zealand ends up being the first region to get access, and their "midnight" corresponds to 3am PT / 6am ET / 11am GMT on November 18th.

Therefore, if people want to play the game as early as possible, they'll need to be in New Zealand - and the "New Zealand Trick" refers to changing your region in your console's settings, providing slightly early access to GTA 6.

There's always been a lot of chatter online about how Xbox doesn't really care about you "moving to New Zealand" to get around release times, but that's technically not the case. Xbox's terms and conditions specifically state that trying to "circumvent regional content restrictions" is prohibited, and this is mentioned a few times in documentation:

The official answer is yes - Xbox could take whatever kind of actions they wanted against an account that was found breaking the rules to play GTA 6 early on Xbox Series X and S. It could result in a warning, a suspension, a ban, or anything else they see fit.

You might also get away with it, as have the majority of people with many other games in the past, but it's still something you should only do at your own risk. We don't recommend breaking the rules just to play a game a few hours early, but we're also not naive enough to think that people won't be trying it come November 18th!

Something to also keep in mind with this is that spoilers will likely begin hitting the web from the New Zealand release time on November 18th (if not earlier). At that point, we expect all kinds of footage and screenshots to begin flooding social media, so you may want to have a bit of a digital detox until the 19th if you don't want to see anything.

Anyway, we know this is a hot topic, and feel free to share your thoughts about it in the comments below. The decision is up to you - but just know that you are running a risk by "moving to New Zealand", however small it might appear to be.

#4061. What remains of canned Portal prequel white whale F-Stop is now fully playable thanks to modders and some big leaks

If you're something of a Portal or Half-Life head, you'll probably already be familiar with F-Stop, an unreleased Portal prequel that remained quite mysterious for many years. Back in 2020, a much deeper look was revealed in a semi-official capacity, revealing a pretty neat concept (that isn't so dissimilar to that of Superliminal). Now, all these years later, assets and source code for the game has leaked, and what exists of F-Stop is fully playable.

As spotted by Kotaku, the Valve Cut Content team and a number of leakers have been able to put together a playable version of F-Stop so that you can try it out for yourself. Mechanically, it works like so: you take a picture of an object, and said object disappears, turning it into a photo. You can then use this photo to rematerialise the object, sometimes changing the scale of it to help you navigate particular puzzles. It's cool! Just not something Valve thought was worth going all in on, evidently.

So the story goes, Valve overlord Gabe Newell did actually quite like the early version of the game that never was, it's just it didn't test all that well. I do kind of think that this is a lesson in not always listening to test audiences; the aforementioned Superliminal really is quite similar in execution, even tonally it's on the same kind of wavelength, and it ended up being quite a tight little experience that ended up being received quite positively, generally. In the end, bits of F-Stop were Frankensteined into Portal 2, so, at least we got that out of it!

The reason for the delay in being able to play F-Stop in this unofficial capacity is because of the crucial source code and map data. Back in August about 12TB of Steam data leaked, but that only contained the assets for F-Stop. Mods in the Valve Cut Content Discord server said that the person who leaked the F-Stop mapsrc asked for $1000 before just handing over the data in any case. Glad they did, $1000 bucks is a lot, I wouldn't pay it myself. Cool little bit of history to be found here, shame it never materialised in the way it was meant to.

#4060. "It's Terrific" - Take-Two Boss Acknowledges Zelda Remake's High Score Ahead Of GTA VI Launch

There's been a lot of conversation online about the Zelda remake and Grand Theft Auto going head-to-head this month.

GamesBeat has now asked the Take-Two Interactive boss Strauss Zelnick what he thinks about this and Ocarina of Time's current Metacritic score of 96/100.

He politely responded, stating the game's score is "terrific" and Nintendo should be "very proud of the title".

As for the idea of the two games competing against each other, the CEO of Rockstar's parent company didn't really acknowledge any direct "competition", but more broadly, believes "you compete against everything and nothing" in the entertainment business.

"In the entertainment business, you compete against everything and nothing. Everything because there’s so many ways consumers can spend their time, and nothing because if there’s nothing good out there, people don’t need to consume any of it. It’s like food; like food could be bad, but you still are going to be hungry. But in the case of entertainment, it’s not a must-have; it’s a want to have. So it’s our job to make the best entertainment on earth. When we do that, people will show up for it.”

In his words, if it's the "best entertainment on earth", then "people will show up for it".

While Zelda's Ocarina remake has done tremendously well for Nintendo, and early reports suggest its sales are off to a positive start in certain locations, Grand Theft Auto VI (at least for now) has been labelled the most anticipated launch of all time. Presales of the new entry have already exceeded expectations, and it's a digital-only release, with retail copies sold as a "code-in-a-box" release.

And if you're wondering about the possibility of a Switch 2 version, Nintendo of America's president has recently said it's a "conversation for Take-Two and Rockstar". Earlier this week, Rockstar also confirmed GTA VI will run at 30fps on PlayStation 5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X|S. It will be available on Xbox One through Xbox Cloud Gaming, too.

#4059. PlayStation wins "hall of shame" award from consumer rights group

Choice, an Australian consumer rights organization, has named Sony Interactive Entertainment as one of its annual "hall of shame" award winners. Alongside a vocal group of gamers, Choice is calling out PlayStation for failing to give players ownership rights to digital games, a problem that will be much worse with the impending end of physical games on the platform.

PlayStation wins "the Shonky Award for asking us to pay to play, but not own," Choice says in its write-up. According to Sony Interactive Entertainment, the organization argues, "you don’t actually own the movies and games that you buy as a digital download instead of a disc. Instead, you’re buying a license to access the content via Sony’s various digital storefronts, such as the PlayStation Store."

In effect, PlayStation is offering nothing more than long-term rentals for digital games, since it can simply revoke those licenses at any time. That fear will be intimately familiar to players who've been following campaigns like Stop Killing Games, and it's not an arbitrary concern – after all, as Choice notes, Sony did just delist several hundred digital films, revoking digital purchases with no refunds as they did so.

"You can't protect your licensed media based on the current EULA, and there won’t be any alternatives once the discs go away," Choice concludes. "You'll own nothing."

That lack of ownership may be a feature, not a bug, of PlayStation's planned end of physical media. The company still makes significant money on physical releases of its biggest games, but analysts argue that it's more interested in "control" of the market. No discs means no used games, which means Sony can take a cut of every transaction and set prices – alongside third-party publishers – without worrying about competition from secondhand markets.

Choice's Shonky Awards have been ongoing since 2006, and have sporadically included gaming companies in the annual hall of shame. In 2023, it named and shamed the Xbox Mini Fridge for failing to actually cool anything while drawing more power than a full-sized fridge. In 2013, when EA's always-online SimCity reboot launched to global server issues, Choice called out a problem particular to Australian players: the support line charged $2.48 per minute, "making people pay to complain."

Publisher and developer Rockstar Games has announced that preloading for the highly anticipated GTA 6 is now available to everyone who pre-ordered digitally.

In other words, if you pre-ordered the game via the PS Store, you can now begin downloading and installing the game on your PS5 to ensure it's ready to go come launch day.

The news comes alongside a brief new trailer, which includes a few new snippets of GTA 6 in action as well as the song Blood In Your Eyes by Tove Lo, which is part of the game's licensed soundtrack.

Those who have pre-ordered the code-in-a-box version of the game will need to wait a little longer to begin preloading, and you can read more about that in our GTA 6 Release Times and Preload guide through the link.

It'll definitely be worth preloading the game as soon as possible, because the install size is pretty enormous, so it may take a while for you to get the download done.

#4057. Dune: Awakening's seasonally appropriate Blood and Ice expansion gets a December release date, and in a plus for preservation, an offline mode this month

December is certainly going to be the month of Dune. The biggest Dune of Dunecember will obviously go to Dune: Part 3, which is Duen out December 18th. A little bit before that, however, is a well-timed free expansion coming to Dune: Awakening. It's called Blood and Ice, which sounds gross, but hey, I guess free blood and ice isn't entirely a bad thing?

"The expansion introduces the Polar Sink, an entirely new survival map where everything you've learned about surviving in the desert will be put to the test," explains a Steam blog post. "Instead of protecting yourself from extreme heat, you'll need to find ways to stay warm. The technology you've developed to survive the desert won't be enough here, and you'll need to upgrade your equipment, gather new resources, and adapt your strategies to survive the cold."

You'll find two biomes in the Polar Sink, the tundra and the ice cap, the former being where you'll kick off your time in this expansion. "While conditions here are more manageable than on the ice cap itself, these families won't welcome anyone interfering with their operations," the blog notes. Your main goal is to get the ice cap and gather up all of its valuable resources, namely, ice! Said ice can then be used to "cool your base equipment and speed up production."

Apparently you'll get about 35 more hours of "new progression, along with new vehicle modules, augments, and specialization traits," out of the expansion, and there are plans for future updates that'll give you reason to come back to the Polar Sink in Duen time. Beyond that, there is also a new cosmetic store, which lets you purchase "optional cosmetic items, including outfits, vehicle variants, and additional ways to customize your bases." I'm sure this will go down well.

Perhaps most importantly, this November will see the arrival of offline mode, meaning you don't need an internet connection to play it. Hopefully if (probably when (sorry to be a pessimist (realist))) the servers go down, this means it'll still be playable. Character copying so that you can copy your character from multiplayer servers to single-player will be coming in January, alongside full cross-play. Lots coming essentially!

#4056. GTA 6 Will Be Playable On Xbox One Through Xbox Cloud Gaming

Rockstar also confirms GTA 6 will run at 30FPS

Update [Tue 10th Nov 2026, 4:03pm]: According to The Verge's Tom Warren, he believes GTA 6 will only be playable on Xbox Cloud Gaming on consoles, with PC and mobile excluded. Xbox Wire recently posted the three ways to play GTA 6 on Xbox. We've updated the article to reflect this.

Original Story: Buying current-gen Xbox hardware isn't cheap these days, and with GTA 6 is now confirmed to be running 30FPS on Xbox Series X|S, what chance would an Xbox One have of running the game, even if it had launched for previous generation tech?

Well, thanks to Rockstar's pre-load notes, we now know GTA 6 will be playable on Xbox One through Xbox Cloud Gaming at Xbox Series S graphics settings. This means those of you who can't upgrade to Xbox Series can still play GTA 6 on November 18th November 19th!

"The game will also be available via XBOX Cloud Gaming on XBOX Series X|S and XBOX One consoles, utilizing XBOX Series S graphics settings. And as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay. GTAVI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and XBOX."

You'll of course be at the mercy of Xbox's fresh Cloud Gaming time caps, limiting how long you can stream games depending on your Xbox Game Pass subscription. You can purchase additional time beyond your allotted amount, and if you're still stuck on Xbox One, topping up your cloud gaming hours could work out cheaper than buying an Xbox Series console. A free ad-supported version of Xbox Cloud Gaming is also currently in testing.

However, there may be a catch. According to Tom Warren, it appears that playing GTA 6 via Xbox Cloud Gaming will be restricted to Xbox consoles. If you were planning on streaming the game on PC or mobile, you may need to think again.

"I also incorrectly assumed it would be like every other Xbox Cloud Gaming title and support phone, PC, web, and TV streaming too. GTA 6 is unlike any other game, so clearly an exception has been made here to restrict to just Xbox consoles"

In a recent Xbox Wire post, Microsoft adds weight to Warren's claims, stating the three ways you can play GTA 6 on Xbox:

But back to Rockstar's notes, the Scotland-based dev did indeed confirm that both Xbox and PlayStation devices will target 30FPS whilst pushing the hardware "to their absolute limits" to play GTA 6. My advice would be to give your Xbox a good clean before release. You don't want your console overheating just when the game finally comes out!

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants."

Pre-loading GTA 6 is live now, even if you don't officially own the game yet. If you'd like to know how, then be sure to check out our preload guide featured at the bottom of this article.

Here are some tips for beating one of Phantom Blade Zero's most challenging bosses, the Blizzard Blademaster

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Phantom Blade Zero Blizzard Blademaster is arguably one of the hardest bosses in the entire game, thanks to his lightning-fast attacks and ice powers. He can freeze you solid, which is extremely irritating as there are very few ways to counter it other than simply not getting hit by any of the Blademaster's attacks – just be glad this is a one-phase fight! But don't despair as he can be beaten with a bit of guidance and the right equipment, so here's what you need to do to defeat the Blizzard Blademaster.

Blizzard Blademaster is an optional boss found at the end of the Four Guardians' Mirror area in the frozen part of Meigu Lake – bear in mind you can only get here if you've opened the Phantom Blade Zero Crimson Manor!

Despite being optional and rather unforgiving with his powerful freezing strikes and dashes, I still highly recommend finding and defeating this boss, both for story purposes and because you get his excellent ice sword as a reward.

Make sure your weapons are fully upgraded (I used the Baishan Stormswords, Armybreaker, Bashpole, and Ink Cut in case that helps) and that you've got the best Phantom Blade Zero Accessories equipped. Otherwise, this is what you should do to beat him:

Persevere and you'll eventually overcome Blizzard Blademaster, getting his fantastic two-handed sword Whiteshadow that lets you freeze your enemies too. Hopefully you also collected every clothing item in the Four Guardians' Mirror area to get the Boy's Worn Outfit, letting you immediately Soul Temper Whiteshadow too.

I won't spoil exactly what happens next, but you also finally get to use the Yin and Yang crystal eyes which finally leads to the end of the 'Secrets at the Heart of the Lake' side quest, which provides some additional story context and gives you a Soul Tempering item for one of your Phantom Edges.

As an ice-cold boss, you could try the Phantom Blade Zero Flaming Mane weapon. If you're still struggling with this boss, make sure you find as many Long Pillars as you can to fight the Phantom Blade Zero Gold-Masked One for practice.

#4054. Gag Order is a co-op, SCP-ish horror shooter about surviving as best you can against some nasty, tentacle covered cephalopod creatures

Don't let it touch me, please and thank you

What makes Carrion interesting obviously lies in playing as the monster in a horror game rather than being the one chased down by it. The game's nasty tentacle monster still gives me the heebie jeebies, so I really would hate to be hunted by one. This is where I point you towards Gag Order, a shooter where you are in fact hunted by a disgusting cephalopod creature all while tracking down a distress signal.

Gag Order is not designed to be played solo, it feels wrong to call it friendslop given how unfriendly it is in vibes, but it does feel like it fits into a similar lineage as Lethal Company at the very least. In it, you are a research lab's Guardian Unit member, and you get a distress call "from one of the core parts of the complex." Upon arrival, the atmosphere is rotten, and you quickly come to understand that you are not equipped for what you have to deal with.

The solution, then, is to take care of those nightmare-inducing cephalopod creatures. Except during the first phase of a run, it sounds like they're invincible. Your guns do seem to be able to fend them off at the very least, but it's the second phase, which is geared around a "fast paced team-bossight" where it sounds like you'll be trying to take these things down. I'm not quite sure what the process is to get between those two phases, but I'm quite fond of the vibes on display.

It feels a touch reminiscent of 2000s shooters with some slightly contemporary mechanical sensibilities. I'm fond of the light SCP vibes it has going on, alongside the faint surrealness of certain elements like a bunch of crows hanging out in an abandoned office building. Creepy! Good looking stuff. Gag Order is apparently due out by the end of 2026, though we're obviously getting close there, so it's worth keeping an eye on it by throwing it a wishlist on Steam, if it takes your fancy.

#4053. As if the injury descriptions weren't already ghastly enough in Dwarf Fortress, the legendary outpost builder is getting a "meat biome"

"Lots of meat terrain - muscle, bone, vertebral walls, sinew, sphincters."

Legendary outpost builder Dwarf Fortress is getting a meat biome. A terrible netherworld of bone and artery. A sunken redoubt of gristle and gizzard. An appalling labyrinth of squirt and squelch. Honestly, the biggest shock here is that Dwarf Fortress doesn't appear to have a meat biome already. It certainly has plenty of florid descriptions of fatal injuries.

These foul omens arrive care of a massive "Future of the Fortress" thread on the Bay 12 forums, in which studio co-founder (and prominent genAI disliker) Tarn "Toady One" Adams fields questions about the on-going development. As a forum thread, it's not a formal news source, so please season these tales of gutsy geology with whatever Condiment of Scepticism you consider appropriate.

There's no date for when the new biome might arrive, but Adams says it'll likely exist underground, and will be revolting. "Lots of meat terrain - muscle, bone, vertebral walls, sinew, sphincters," he promised. "We would have rivers of blood/fluids if we ever get to the fluid update, but no new fluids as it stands. We had thrown out the idea for maple syrup style taps on the vertebral walls for cosmic spinal fluid but alas, this is not in the game." At the very least, there won't be any meat trees, but you can mine the meat for resources.

Adams doesn't discuss the origins of the meat biome in the thread – is it more of a headless, fungal phenomenon, or is there some kind of huge mammalian cadaver down there? If it's the latter, one consolation is that the meat biome can't be resurrected. "Ha ha, I don't think regular meat can be animated currently?" Adams remarked in response to a question about biomes of squirming, zombified meat. "So probably not."

The bulk of the conversation around Dwarf Fortress at present concerns forthcoming changes to the magic system, together with how arcane knowledge is categorised, transmitted, preserved and lost throughout each procedurally generated world. There's a lot of speculative chat about that in the Future of the Fortress thread, too much to cleanly summarise. It's saying something about the density and stature of Dwarf Fortress that the addition of flesh caves feels like an afterthought.

Developer Bay 12's current plans for the game also include a crystal biome, which I would say is the nicer option, but then I remembered that this is Dwarf Fortress, the game in which you might end up getting besieged by the ghosts of the very children you callously sent to hunt down a wild elephant. There is absolutely going to be something in the crystal biome that gives you nightmares. Dazzling, prismatic nightmares.

#4050. Xbox Vs. PS5: GTA 6 Specs Revealed, And These Are The Biggest Differences

"Pushing both platforms to their absolute limits"

Rockstar Games has today lifted the lid on a bunch of specs for both the Xbox and PS5 versions of GTA 6, revealing some of the biggest differences (and similarities) between playing the game on each platform.

The most notable bit of information is that every single console runs the game at 30FPS. Regardless of whether you're playing on Xbox Series S, Xbox Series X, PS5 or even PS5 Pro, the max you're getting is 30 frames per-second.

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants."

There will obviously be resolution differences between each platform, but Rockstar has yet to reveal these details. Expect the Series S to fare the worst, the PS5 Pro to fare the best, and the Series X and PS5 to be pretty much equal.

Rockstar does say that GTA 6 "plays best" on PS5 though (and let's not forget that Sony appears to have a marketing deal in place with Rockstar Games for this release), highlighting the differences between the PS5 and Xbox versions as being "high-fidelity haptic feedback" for the PS5 DualSense controllers, improved spatial audio rendering, and bizarrely, improved load times. That last one is surely just a minimal advantage at best!

Grand Theft Auto VI for PS5 includes high-fidelity haptic feedback fully integrated across the game on DualSense controllers and adjustable via accessibility settings, improved spatial audio rendering so all in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D Audio, and improved load times, making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

Beyond that, the PS5 Pro version will benefit from improved clarity via PSSR along with ray-traced shadows.

However, the Xbox version has one massive benefit in the form of Xbox Cloud Gaming. It seems Xbox will be the only platform offering cloud streaming for GTA 6 at launch, making it an exclusive of sorts - at least for now. The bizarre bit is that it only appears to be for consoles, rather than other devices like PCs and mobiles.

The Xbox and PS5 versions will also support Remote Play (allowing you to cast your game to another device from your console). Nothing has been said about Quick Resume yet on Xbox, but we assume it'll be supported as well.

Ultimately, GTA 6 is bound to run great regardless of whether you buy it on Xbox or PlayStation, and the "plays best on PS5" differences mentioned by Rockstar Games appear to be minor advantages rather than major ones.

We can't wait for footage to start appearing online next week — especially for the Xbox Series S version — and here's hoping it's going to live up to the ridiculous hype that's been fueling the past decade. Not long to wait at all now!

#4049. Skyblivion modders reveal a former volunteer is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000" over work on the unofficial Oblivion remake project

"I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release"

The team behind Oblivion remake mod Skyblivion are being threatened with legal action by a former volunteer on the project, according a video posted by current lead Kyle 'Rebelzize' Rebel. The situation looks like it'll need resolving before the mod, which was originally set to release last year, can finally make its way out of the Imperial City sewers.

"Recently, a former volunteer who contributed to Skyblivion’s development departed the project," the Skyblivion team outlined in a written statement and a YouTube video presented by Rebel. "We want to be completely transparent with the community about what has happened since their departure. After they left the project, we had several discussions regarding the continued use and maintenance of his work. The main disagreement centered on their objection to our decompilation of parts of their work — a necessary step our team took to maintain functionality and fix issues in systems already built into the project after access to the original source code repository was revoked."

"To protect ourselves from more stress and try and ensure a clean break, we decided to take the high road," Rebel explained in the video. "We have removed that work entirely. Thankfully due to some of our volunteers stepping up and simply learning new skill sets, as well as help from prominent Skyrim modders and permissions to use and integrate existing Skyrim mods, we've been able to implement replacements that we think fit Skyblivion's needs, in some cases even better than what we had before."

However, Rebel and co claim that despite them making it "clear multiple times to this former volunteer that we have removed their contributions", the ex-Skyblivion dev is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000". They claim that the ex-volunteer's legal threats "demand personal information of multiple volunteers [on Skyblivion] including full names and addresses". Rebel noted that the team see these demands as "something that we are simply not willing to share with someone that we don't even know" and feel are "just completely disproportionate for what's really going on".

The modders say they've consulted with legal counsel already and have a lawyer on standby if necessary. Though, since said lawyer's services will - the Skyblivion team claim - cost €2,500, they've put out a call for anyone with "a background in IP law or GDPR law" willing to offer them pro bono legal aid to get in touch via the mod's website.

"Please don't turn this into any kind of witch hunt, despite this very unfortunate situation," Rebel said in closing. "We don't wish ill on a former volunteer over all this and I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release, which is really what we're working towards. You will hear more from us soon on the actual release."

This situation makes it two years running that Skyblivion's found itself engulfed in drama during the final months of what's supposed to be its release year. In 2025, former volunteer Dee Keyes had a public disagreement with the project's leads over whether releasing the mod that year was a reasonable or achievable goal. Skyblivion was subsequently delayed into 2026.

This past weekend, Keyes tweeted a response to the Skyblivion team's statement on the alleged legal threats. "I've had my issues with the project and left because of it, but I left knowing that my work would remain with [Skyblivion] (happily so) and didn't want to hurt the project's progress," he wrote. "I understand [the former volunteer] being upset, but I really don't see why they'd go so far as to demand their work ripped out."

Here's hoping the Skyblivion team and the ex-volunteer can resolve things without all the expense and effort that'd inevitably be necessary if the dispute ends up in court. Given there are now less than two months left of 2026, and Skyblivion's modders have this on their plates on top of any remaining work needed to finish their creation, I'd personally be very surprised if its release doesn't end up being pushed into next year.

#4048. Delve into "a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors" in the latest Fallout 4 quest mod from the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project

A mysterious bunker with out of this world contents

After adding a whole new town to Fallout 4 last month, a group of modders have released another in their long string of extra quests for the RPG. This latest mission revolves around a dungeon delve in the Glowing Sea, where a mysterious bunker's just been unearthed.

"The harsh radioactive winds of the Glowing Sea have uncovered a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors," the group behind the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project (CSEP) declared the description of this latest work, Under The Stars.

A fresh dungeon with a quest attached, the mod tasks you with donning your hazmat suit for a trip to a sunken bunker in the region of post-apocalyptic Boston with the least chill weather. Inside await voiced holotapes and puzzles offering clues as to what went down in this cosy corner of the Commonwealth, plus some new gear to make braving whatever lurks within worth it.

Spoilers: Judging by the screenshots, it looks like the place is an Area 51-esque hidey-hole for evidence of aliens and other cryptic oddities.

If you're unfamiliar, the CSEP lot are responsible for a bunch of popular Fallout 4 quest mods based around the likes of deadly cults, underground wars, post-apocalyptic detective work, and Brotherhood of Steel drama. While Under The Stars doesn't look have been as big an undertaking as those, that previous form points to it being an expertly-crafted addition that'll slot seamlessly into the game.

The modders have put Under The Stars together as part of a community-hosted modding jam called Fallout Flood, with this latest one based around the theme of being underground. Among the other works to have come out of it thus far are another Fallout 4 quest mod dubbed Stranded - The Oasis, a dungeon full of funky rats called the S'Laven, and a new robot enemy you can wear as a hat. It's also produced a New Vegas quest mod about exploring an abandoned NCR railway, so seems to have been very productive gathering of modding minds.

To give Under The Stars a go, your copy of Fallout 4 will need to have the Automatron and Vault-Tec Workshop DLCs.

#4046. It's Official, Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Has Sold Over 5 Million Copies In 4 Days

Nintendo has announced that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has sold a total of 5.2 million units in just four days.

This number includes 810,000 copies sold in Japan alone, and makes Ocarina of Time the fastest-selling Nintendo-published Switch 2 game since the console's launch. For added context, the N64 original sold an overall total of 7.6 million units, according to Video Game Sales wiki.

This also makes it the second highest-selling Switch 2 game, with initial sales putting it above Donkey Kong Bananza's lifetime sales at 5.05 million (as of 30th September 2026). The best-selling Switch 2 game remains Mario Kart World at 16.48 million.

It's not clear what the digital/physical split is at the time of writing, though we should have a slightly better picture of this once Famitsu releases the Japanese boxed charts later this week.

Nintendo Co., Ltd. (HQ: Kyoto, Minami-ku, Japan; President and Representative Director: Shuntaro Furukawa, “Nintendo” hereafter) announced that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2 sold over 5.2 million units worldwide (including 810,000 units sold in Japan) in the first four days following its launch on November 5, 2026.

This is the highest global sales for any Nintendo-published Nintendo Switch 2 game in its first four days.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2, released worldwide on November 5, is a full remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, originally released for Nintendo 64 in 1998. Link travels between two time periods, as Young Link and Adult Link, making use of different abilities and items available in each period to progress through his adventure. Developed for Nintendo Switch 2, the game features reimagined visuals and enhanced playability, while preserving the experience of the original game.

The game also supports ZELDA NOTES, a service available within the Nintendo Switch App for compatible smart devices. By using ZELDA NOTES, players can access a variety of features that support gameplay.

In the UK, it was confirmed that Ocarina of Time was the second biggest physical launch in series history, coming in just behind Tears of the Kingdom. It stormed to the top of the charts to become the biggest physical video game launch of 2026 (so far – hi, GTA).

As for our review, we awarded Ocarina of Time a 9/10, stating it to be "the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time":

"Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the experience with stunning visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio. Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time."

#4045. Fewer genAI clones of "someone else's specific game" should flood the net going forwards, as Anthropic tell Claude to stop messing with some stuff other people own

It will still let people generate "original" games using the tech

Anthropic have told their genAI tool Claude to start ducking requests from users to recreate or clone existing games, following a flood of folks using the tech to generate six-fingered remakes. Instead of risking infringing on the intellectual property of series or titles that companies which aren't Anthropic own, Claude will instead restrict itself to only generating "original" games slopped together based on whatever data it's drawing on.

"We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Anthropic staffer Addy Osmani wrote on not Twitter in response to a rando with a cat profile picture having spotted the change.

"Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working," Osmani continued. "We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way." Game Developer reached out to Anthropic for confirmation and were pointed to Osmani's post.

The change should make it harder to add to the horde of genAI-powered decomps, recomps, and ports which have hit the net recently. It's hardly a surprising one, given studios like Bethesda have seemingly had to take matters into their own lawyers' hands to get the likes of an AI-generated Fallout game taken offline, with games that've just been ripped wholesale or barely tweaked likely on even more perilous ground. That said, not every corp's responded to the DIY decompilation craze by immediately taking legal action.

There's a serious degree of irony to Anthropic slapping Claude and telling it stealing is bad. One of the ways the company develop and train their genAI models is by scraping publicly available data from the internet via a web crawler.

So, some nicking of stuff is bad, little bot people keep asking to regurgitate stuff into slop they can then try to pass off as something they've created. But not all nicking of stuff, lest our whole business be on rather shaky ground.

It's unlikely this move from Anthropic does much to convince actual developers of original games they're safe to put demos of their games out prior to release, without risking dickheads using genAI to clone said demo and potentially release a slop version in rapid fashion, but one can dream of that genie being put back in the bottle someday.

#4044. GTA 6 on PS5 Is PS Store's Most Pre-Ordered Digital Game in History

It was always going to be big, but with a week until release, Rockstar has now confirmed that GTA 6 is the most pre-ordered digital game in PS Store history.

Confirmation comes courtesy of the PS Blog, in a post from Sony’s Tim Turi.

“GTA 6 is now the most pre-ordered game in the history of PS Store. Given this unprecedented demand, we’ve joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start pre-loading the game nine days early, so they’re ready to play on launch day. We’ve also adopted a rolling midnight launch by country, beginning at 12:00AM NZDT in New Zealand and running across the globe as respective countries hit midnight on 19th November.”

You can learn more about when you’ll be able to play in our dedicated GTA 6 release times guide, so keep that bookmarked for 19th November.

Digital pre-orders for GTA 6 have been available since 25th June, so Rockstar has had a long time to build up numbers.

It’s worth reiterating that physical versions are following a “code-in-box” format, so there’s less incentive to purchase at retail, too.

(Although in a recent Push Square poll, a remarkable 23% of our readers did say they’d be plumping up for the boxed version.)

Record-breaking pre-orders like this are significant as the PS Store has been selling digital games for over a decade now; that it’s set a new record with over a week to spare and hype still building is remarkable.

While we don’t have actual numbers, Rockstar’s said they’re “exceeding” its external expectations.

Analyst firm Sensor Tower predicts 9.69 million pre-orders have been placed, with an astonishing 75% of those sales commanded by the PS5 version.

It’s worth noting that this milestone comes at a time of deep unrest among PS5 players, who’ve continuously spammed the platform holder with proclamations of ‘No Disc, No Buy’ in the aftermath of its decision to stop shipping physical games in 2028.

Sony recently reported year-over-year increases to its monthly active users, during a period in which enthusiasts mobilised a “blackout” of its platform.

Irrespective of fan frustration, it looks like Rockstar’s latest open world is days away from registering the biggest digital launch in industry history.

The game is also now the most pre-ordered Microsoft Store title ever

We're getting a whole ton of GTA 6 details coming out today, and Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has taken to social media to issue a statement about the game's pre-orders, as well as a new 10-year partnership with its publisher Take-Two.

Sharma didn't share any specific details about the partnership in her post, but we did cover the deal at the beginning of October, which allows Take-Two to develop and sell Xbox-compatible products across all Xbox devices. Beyond handling Rockstar's GTA and Red Dead Redemption IPs, Take-Two Interactive also manages 2K and Zynga titles. If Sharma intends to entertain more than a billion players every day, striking up a cloud streaming deal with Take-Two is a great place to start.

#4042. Fix up towering robots while battle rages outside in Bay 12: Mech Repair, a first-person job sim with some handsome heavy duty analog tech

The most important thing to know about Bay 12: Mech Repair is that these are mechs of the MechWarrior or possibly Patlabor school – that is, basically WW2 tanks on hydraulic legs, with cockpits full of switches and wireframe displays. Their bodies are assemblages of pistons and reactors. They are not biomechs like the ones in Evangelion. An Evangelion Repair game would be… different. Less industrial, more Oedipal. You would dread removing the smallest piece of housing.

Which isn't to say that Bay 12: Mech Repair represents life on Easy Street, exactly. There's a big war happening outside, its fortunes palpable in the minced leg joints and pocked torsos of the war-bots lowered into your hangar. You're also fed details about the lives of pilots when you accept a work order. Lieutenant Iona Vale of the 3rd Recon Company says there's "left leg hesitation after extended operation", especially at higher temperatures. That sure sounds like a thing that could get Lieutenant Iona Vale killed.

It's not clear whether you can diagnose faults incorrectly, and shape the progress of the conflict, but the context brings extra emotional charge to what might otherwise be a cosy process of glueing together very expensive Air-Fix models, for all the sense of scale.

Bay 12: Mech Repair follows a familiar flow, as job sims go. Banged-up Iron Giants arrive in a steady procession. You figure out what's wrong with them based on scans, pilot reports, and so forth. Then you get out there with a welder, drill and spanner to make it right. Busted parts can be salvaged for scrap for custom components. Completed work orders net you credits that must be divided between restocking your inventory and buying new tools.

You also have the option of clearing away rust and applying a new paintjob. I'm fascinated to know if this has any real impact on either the story or your fortunes, because I guarantee that I am going to spend far more time obsessing over dazzle camouflage than giving the ol' actuators a haircut.

Read more on Steam. The devs, Crimson Herring Studios, are them wot did Sovereign Syndicate, an apparently decent Victorian fantasy RPG that we never found time to review. Look, I am not made of thumbs and eyeballs. As for the daunting possibility of an Evangelion Fixing Sim, the recently announced Valkyrie Iteration gets into some of the squirming detail, there.

#4041. You can make a vampire hunter who's afraid of the dark, disease and small spaces in Hunter: The Reckoning - Deathwish, and that's surely the best way to play

A month or two back I penned a 1500 word whine about feeling too powerful in Blood of Dawnwalker. "Gimme a vampire sim in which I'm a pathetic vein-nibbling goblin," I wrote, using many more adjectives than that. Well, never let it be said that I'm biased against vampires, for I am equally keen to play an RPG in which I am the least capable vampire hunter in the universe. A vampire hunter who screams when he wakes up with his hair over his face. A vampire hunter who has to spray the vampires with antibac before staking them.

An RPG like Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish, perhaps, which presents you with a choice of Advantages and Flaws when creating a character. You have to balance these out on a gnarly weighing scale, before they'll let you through the game's front door. Here is a video showing all that off, together with a lot of sixpacks.

The Advantage/Flaw system looks familiar on the surface. Advantages include Warrior, which gives you +15% chance of a critical hit, or Charmer, which gives you a +1 to Persuasion skill checks. Flaws include clumsy, bad reputation, fear of darkness, hypochondriac, and claustrophobia.

I don't know much about the tabletop game on which Deathwish is based, and the video skims the detail here, but I suspect the last three Flaws will boil down to something like "-1 Constitution in Unlit Closets". Still, I really enjoy the idiocy of going up against crypt-dwelling undead while being unable to tolerate shadows, small spaces, and disease. In general, I'd love it if Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish steered well away from any possibility of simply overpowering the vamps, to say nothing of the werewolves and other creatures of the night.

This appears to be the idea: devs Teyon have stressed their desire to make something more story and investigation-driven, after the stomping gibfest that was RoboCop: Rogue City. As narrative designer Mateusz Działowski put it in a previous dev diary, they've "switched from action with RPG elements into RPG with action elements". Amongst other things, you'll need to put together a team of fellow would-be slayers, each with secrets and traumas, and gather clues about best tactics while roaming the game's condensed and shiny New York City. You can read more about it all on Steam.

#4040. itch.io will soon let you filter games with genAI disclosures out of your search results on the site, after admitting it was previously "critically lacking"

itch.io has unfortunately, much like Steam, long had an issue with genAI content being uploaded in droves, drowning out perfectly good games made by human hands. The apparent standard method against this, voluntary genAI disclosure, has been itch's primary tool to combat this wave of low-quality slop, but hasn't worked out too well; itch revealed a few days ago that 'the number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past two months'. Now, in attempts to further combat this, beyond just game assets requiring a genAI disclosure to upload as they have for two years, itch will be expanding the mandatory disclosure to tabletop games, books, comics, and soundtracks, as well as adding a 'no AI' filter directly into the search function.

itch noted in this announcement that its previous moderation of genAI use in projects had been "critically lacking", presumably referring to the unfathomable exponential increase in games being uploaded in the past few months by people who don't give a fuck about creating anything themselves and happily contribute to the death of the planet. itch went on to post "Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop" which, I mean, sure, cool! And, look, as many, many people in itch's replies have pointed out, this is not the same as outright banning AI.

Unfortunately, my question at that point becomes: how? itch is not Steam, not a storefront backed by a gigantic corporation with support staff and quality assurance (which, you know, hasn't helped Steam much either). itch is one full-time employee with several contractors and volunteers. If there is a site-wide ban on genAI, people who use genAI will just start lying and sneaking it into their projects anyway. So, then, users just report the offenders, surely? This then requires a manual verification system, which, as is suggested by the sheer amount of games being uploaded every day, is just not feasible, let alone for a team as small as itch. And, frankly, I don't have a better solution here! This is fucked! What itch is doing is, currently, kinda the best it can right now?

itch is a beautiful thing that allows for people who just want to start making games, making art, making music, making books, to have a free space to share it with the world, and gain eyes on their work as well as necessary feedback to improve. It's less of a store and more of a forum for creators and self-published games to interact, guide one another to new, niche, cool shit. Hell, I made a visual novel and posted it on there, becoming another one of those millions of people for whom itch is a valuable platform for first creations. To have this vital space on a path to ruin as a result of the same vile tech that is also on the verge of pushing the global economy over a cliff due to its creators being caught in their multi-year lies is not a future I hope for itch. This is a step in the right direction, and one I genuinely hope pans out well for it in the long run.

#4039. What Happens When Two Games Have The Same Title? Indie Publisher Reveals Heartwarming Answer

"I signed their game and now we're launching both"

With so many games releasing these days, it must be so difficult to come up with a completely unique title without encroaching on another developer's work.

Case in point, an indie game by the name of Piece by Piece from publisher No More Robots launched earlier this year on Steam, but in an amusing twist of fate, another game called Piece by Piece came out in the same week.

Now, this isn't the case of a washed up dev blatantly copying another for easy money – both titles here are radically different to one another, but they just happen to share the same name.

If this were a big publisher like EA, Ubisoft, or even Nintendo, you could easily imagine that it would be taking action to force a name change. That is if it doesn't work to remove the duplicate game from sale altogether.

However, as highlighted by Mike Rose from No More Robots, the developer of the other Piece by Piece game couldn't afford to bring it to Switch. So, in what is no doubt a remarkably kind gesture, No More Robots did it for them.

I have some 🌟feel-good news🌟 to share today! Earlier this year we launched a game called Piece by Piece. In the same week, *another* game called Piece by Piece came out I heard from the dev that they couldn't afford to bring their game to Switch. So I signed their game and now we're launching both

"I have some feel-good news to share today!

"Earlier this year we launched a game called Piece by Piece. In the same week, *another* game called Piece by Piece came out.

"I heard from the dev that they couldn't afford to bring their game to Switch. So I signed their game and now we're launching both."

Both titles are available for pre-order via the Switch eShop ahead of their release on 25th November, and you can also opt for a bundle if you're keen to try out both.

Rose states that Nintendo "absolutely hated this", questioning why both games have the same title during the certification process. We totally understand Nintendo's position on this, but it's wonderful to see that it approved everything in the end. Rose ended his announcement to say "Anyway, mega happy to be helping them out with such a fun thing. Not all publishers are evil, I promise!!".
