#3982. "Arkane is profitable," say Marvel's Blade developers in fiery new statement, "just not profitable enough for Microsoft"

Unionised workers reiterate call for a "solid offer" for Arkane Lyon's future

Unionised workers at Dishonored developers Arkane Lyon have published a fresh statement about the progress of negotiations with Microsoft over the studio's potential closure. Aside from calling on Xbox management to make a redundancy offer proportionate to Microsoft's colossal market value, they accuse the parent company of creating the very economic conditions cited as a reason for closing Arkane, and thereby "sabotaging" development of the forthcoming Marvel's Blade.

Published by French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo - one of two unions who represent workers at Arkane, the other being Printemps écologique, who didn't issue a similar message - the official English translation of the statement begins by insisting that "work on Blade is going fine". It maintains that the game will measure up to previous Arkane Lyon releases, despite the stress of trying to pin down a new owner for the company, after Microsoft announced plans to part ways with Arkane and several other studios back in July. The writers then take Microsoft to task for making an "outrageously low" redundancy offer to Arkane's workers, and further accuse the Xbox company of essentially setting Arkane up to fail by imposing a hiring freeze and depriving the studio of resources.

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the workers write. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist." It asserts that Microsoft froze hiring "for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost", only to then use those delays and extra costs "as a reason to close down the studio". It also claims that Microsoft have "systematically" deprived Arkane of cash, by means of corporate mechanisms the statement doesn't make wholly clear. "Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," the statement adds, without going into detail.

"The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals," the workers continue. They accuse Microsoft of "the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization", citing years of mass layoffs across the Xbox company together with the recent voluntary buyout offering. "Arkane is profitable," they add. "Just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The workers want a "solid offer" from Microsoft regarding the studio's post-Xbox future, declaring that "when the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down is, according to many sources the most profitable in the world, with a net profit of more than 133 Billions of dollars in the past years, it would be the bare minimum to ensure that the redundancy plan offered by Microsoft is on [par] with their means."

If Arkane have to close, the unionised workers call on Microsoft "to release funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation, to make sure that the workers are compensated in line with the loss suffered". They'd like a redundancy payment of €200,000, two years of "redeployment support", a package of "shared resources for training and studio creation", including a residual bonus, and "compensation up to the redundancy payment for independent workers’ contract breach", to safeguard the livelihoods of freelancers and contractors.

The warring parties at Xbox and Arkane have until 11th December this year to figure out a deal. Reportedly, Ubisoft are among those looking to buy Arkane - a source of some concern, given that Ubisoft have also recently closed a number of studios and laid many people off. I'm not sure I'd be waving my wallet around if I were using my other hand to sign pink slips.

#3980. Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has much worse input lag than PS5

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has noticeably worse input lag than on PS5, which could put Nintendo players at a disadvantage in multiplayer.

Digital Foundry's tech review measured multiplayer latency at 81ms when docked and an average of 100ms in portable mode, against 49ms on PS5. Testing used wireless controllers on both consoles (a Switch 2 Pro Controller and a DualSense), and portable results ranged from 83ms at best to 125ms at worst.

Digital Foundry said "responsiveness here simply isn't as good as on other consoles", and described the lag in portable mode as "actually deleterious to performance" (thanks, IGN).

Beyond the lag, Digital Foundry is fairly positive about the port. Multiplayer runs at 60fps most of the time, and if your TV supports VRR, you'll notice the drops less. The campaign is capped at 30fps and resolution is dynamic.

Docked with DLSS on, the game targets 900p, but Digital Foundry saw it drop to 450p in busier scenes, such as the Paris vehicle chase. In portable mode, the target is 720p, with drops to 360p.

It's been 13 years since a Call of Duty game last appeared on Nintendo hardware, with Ghosts on Wii U in 2013. The series' return is the result of a 10-year deal Microsoft offered Nintendo while it sought regulatory approval for its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

If you have a high-end RTX 50-series graphics card then kudos to you. You either got in there early and avoided the massive price hikes that followed, or you managed to get a second mortgage and pick one up anyways. But either way, you're going to want to protect your investment because replacements are hard and expensive to find. And it looks like you really need to protect that investment because there are still regular cases of melting 12+4 pin power cables.

This latest (via Uniko's Hardware) serves as a reminder that getting a cable monitoring solution is a good way to protect your expensive graphics card, as user Edistonian2 notes in a recent reddit thread on the ThermalGrizzly sub. They note that they picked up an RTX 5090 in June and subsequently grabbed a WireView Pro II monitor to keep it safe.

The WireView noted odd current behaviour with two of the pins, while HWInfo said it was fine and a Gemini chat suggested it was an issue with the monitor. I'm sure that's what Nvidia would say, too... So they replace their WireView with a new one, and still get the current issues on pin four. So they removed the cable entirely and the image up top is what was happening on the PSU end of the wire.

They've since picked up another cable and swapped to the other GPU power port on the GPU and so far everything is fine, but it just shows that there are still power issues going on with these cables and a monitoring system can be a worthwhile step in between finding your power leads or plugs melting, or your GPU going up in a puff of smoke.

Now, it's not the cheapest method—the WireView Pro II is $190 at Amazon right now—but that is chump change in relation to the ~$8,000 you might have to spend on a replacement RTX 5090. There are also cheaper alternatives, such as Cooler Master's GPU Shield, which is $50, and the Super Flower 12+4 pin OCP Dongle.

Whichever you choose, as the pricing crisis continues for high-end cards, that's going to be a small price to pay to save something catastrophic happening to your expensive silicon.

#3978. "BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy" argues petition calling on Canadian government to step in

1,662 Canadians have been verified as signing it thus far

Calls for the Canadian government to help ressurect recently shuttered RPG makers BioWare have progressed from a single post by a politician to a petition with enough signatures that it looks set to be presented to the Canadian House of Commons for an official response. So far, 1,662 people from the country of maple syrup and also other things have signed this call for their leaders to consider stepping in.

"BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports to the world in the 21st century, selling tens of millions of units of their video games globally," declares the petition, started by Brendan Routh and authorised by Vancouver Kingsway MP Don Davies.

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," its run of bullet points continues. "BioWare has been shuttered by its American parent company Electronic Arts, now owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partners and BioWare's closure represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

With all of that in mind, the petition calls on the Canadian Government to "provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company". The Canadians who've signed also want their leaders to "protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests" and "champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry".

Thus far, the petition's amassed 1,662 verified signatures from citizens across Canada, putting it above the 500 verified signature threshold required for it to be presented to the country's House of Commons. That'll be followed by the tabling of an official response from the Canadian government.

As with some of the responses from political bodies the likes of the Stop Killing Games campaign have gotten over the years, I find it hard not to see this petition not being greeted with an answer along the lines of 'We do care about this and thank you for raising it, but we're not really gonna do much here'. I think a full BioWare resurrection with government backing is highly unlikely, but finding some way to enshrine the studio's legacy or contribution to Canada's games industry and arts culture seems a lot more easily doable.

A big statue of Blokeshep and Femshep surrounded by their crew of potential allies somewhere in Edmonton, maybe. Or a big stone middle finger that's always required to be aimed at a poster for the next Star Wars film/game/TV show/bit of merch.

#3977. At Dead of Night sequel The Great Hugo is coming "(very) soon"

Baggy Cat Games, the team behind viral FMV horror game At Dead Of Night, has confirmed that a sequel is "coming (very) soon".

At Dead Of Night 2: The Great Hugo picks up where the original game left off and reunites us with Maya as she heads off to investigate a large Tudor manor house.

At Dead Of Night became famous quickly during the pandemic thanks to streamers and content creators like Markiplier, 8-BitRyan, John Wolfe, and DomPlays, who introduced us to Jimmy Hall, a creepy hotel landlord hellbent on recruiting an audience for his late-night comedy show and psychopathic comedy alter ego, Hugo Punch.

The new game, subtitled The Great Hugo, picks up half a decade later.

"Five years later, Maya is still haunted by her experiences in Sea View Hotel," the blurb teases. "Desperate for answers she remembers the ghost box she used in the hotel, left there when she escaped.

"After searching on [auction] sites and in antique shops, she finds a similar looking device, but can’t get it to work. She contacts an old friend and counsellor, Quinn, who had helped her understand her supernatural experiences in the hotel. Quinn recognises the device and knows where they were made - by an inventor who used to live in a large Tudor manor house not far from Sea View - but warns her against trying to get it working. However, Maya ignores his advice and goes on her own investigation."

Quite how long "(very) soon" is, we don't yet know, but we'll keep you posted.

As its slightly cheeky title implies, Playable Archive (a riff on the legendary Playable Teaser created for Hideo Kojima's cancelled Silent Hill game) is a small slice of developer Brian Clarke's much larger cancelled Paranormal Activity game, making it a fascinating window into 'what could have been'.

The Outer Worlds 2 is finally getting its DLC. Obsidian has announced that Side Effects Guaranteed, the first of a "two-part expansion" series, will launch on December 2. The devs had been promising DLC since before launch as part of the RPG's $100 Premium Edition, but you'd be forgiven for worrying that those promises were forgotten amid the massive shakeup at the studio.

The first part of Side Effects Guaranteed will offer a new region to explore on Eden, a boosted level cap with new perks grab, four new flaws to spice up your build, new gear, and an additional radio station. The story will have you working with one of two Sub Rosa agents as you decide what to do with the hibernating crew of a derelict ship.

We spoke with Obsidian about The Outer Worlds 2 DLC shortly after the game's launch last year, and at that time they'd only begun to sketch out plans for the expansion. But at least one thing has carried over from those high-level ideas: "Maybe we'll lean a bit harder into some of the more minor factions, like Sub Rosa, and build them out a little bit," game director Brandon Adler told us in 2025, and that part of the plan seems to have borne out.

But a lot has happened at Obsidian since we had that chat. It's now under Bethesda's direct management and working on a new Fallout game as part of Xbox's big shakeup. Obsidian was not immune to the mass layoffs at the publisher, and seemingly had an Avowed sequel stripped away as Xbox pointed it to return to the more lucrative Fallout franchise.

While The Outer Worlds 2 was one of our favorite games of 2025, it never appeared to make much of a splash among the broader gaming community. Its fans feared that slow sales might lead to the DLC being canceled, and there's still some fear that the expansions have been truncated so Obsidian can move onto Fallout more quickly.

#3975. You can now play Pillars of Eternity and Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire with a controller on PC from start to finish, thanks to a new update open for testing

Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also gotten a makeover

After gifting Pillars of Eternity a turn-based mode for its tenth anniversary, Obsidian have now rolled out full PC controller support for both the RPG and its younger sibling Pillars of Eternity 2: Deadfire. The support, along with some tweaks to Deadfire's turn-based mode, are currently out in public test form.

"You can now play the whole of either game with a controller, from character creation to the end credits (and, in Deadfire, all the way out to naval combat), in both real-time with pause and turn-based mode," the studio wrote in their announcement of the public test going live. "Deadfire’s support builds on the controller scheme from the console editions. Prefer to switch things up? Pick up your mouse and keyboard at any time, and the game follows right along."

"Deadfire’s turn-based mode has also been reworked with the improvements we made for Pillars of Eternity’s turn-based mode: turns now follow each character’s speed, combat is more lethal, and swapping weapons or drinking potions no longer costs your action. You can now switch turn-based mode on or off during a playthrough, and the update brings a long list of fixes across combat, quests, audio, and the interface."

Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are included in the support, along with the Steam Deck and Steam's Big Picture mode. Radial menus have been worked in to allow rapid firing of abilities, spells, and party commands, with the interface also popping up the right button prompts for your controller of choice.

These additions are all part of Patch 1.3.10.0, the full notes for which can be found in the post I've embedded above, alongside instructions on how to get into the public test. The patch also does things like ensure "the description of Fulvano’s Boots is no longer fragmented". I'm glad Obsidian have saved those soles.

The studio haven't put a concrete end date on the test at this point, instead noting it "will run for some time as we continue to update it in preparation for a full release". As it's a test, those jumping in should expect bugs and other funkiness.

#3974. Phantom Blade Zero is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, selling over 4 million copies in three days

Phantom Blade Zero studio S-Game has announced that its debut title has sold more than 4m copies in its first 72 hours on sale. The game's official X account broke the news alongside a celebratory message, though without providing a per-platform breakdown of copies sold.

"Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support!" the developer wrote on X.

Phantom Blade Zero is available on Steam and PlayStation 5, but the 4m figure also includes sales made on the China-exclusive Tencent WeGame PC launcher. Prior to launch, Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott estimated Phantom Blade Zero to have sold over 1m copies before it had even released.

It was always clear the third-person character action game was going to be a hit, we just had to wait for actual figures to be released.

Phantom Blade Zero attracted over 431,000 concurrent players on Steam at launch, a figure that kept risking and rising into the weekend, ultimately settling at a massive 833,921 peak concurrent (via SteamDB). Just in case it wasn't already clear, this is Steam's biggest launch of the year so far, beating the likes of Forza Horizon 6 and far outpacing all other major releases such as Onimusha: Way of the Sword, The Blood of Dawnwalker, and Ace Combat 8.

Despite the very strong opening weekend's numbers, Phantom Blade Zero has not been able to match or exceed the performance of Black Myth: Wukong, 2024's also-Chinese developed triple-A action game, just yet. The breakout hit, estimated to have sold 30m copies since, is one of Steam's largest debuts ever, peaking at 2,415,714 concurrent players at launch.

In Eurogamer's Phantom Blade Zero review, Emma Kent spoke highly of much of the game, but was critical of its underwhelming narrative and lack of consistency, writing: "This game is exceptional in so many areas - the animations, the beautiful environments - and when the combat works, the sense of flow is incredible. Then you walk into a boss battle and feel all that power fade, like you're waiting your turn to get hits in with a wooden sword."

Though, to be honest, sometimes I want to play someone else's game.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith had a wide-ranging chat with The Examined Game recently, touching upon topics like the importance of institutional knowledge, what he liked about Baldur's Gate 3, and what he wants to see in The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. But he also dropped a pithy maxim (and less pithy explanation) about his—and Bethesda's—approach to design in general. Here's what he said.

"If you look at the history of triple-A studios that do sequels… you'll see the best game in a sequence frequently was able to maintain a vision, and was very player-centric-forward: 'You're not playing my game, I'm making your game' kind of thing.

One of the things I've always felt, and [Bethesda] felt it too [is] once we've made a game, it's not ours anymore. It's yours. I, once upon a time, actually had a developer complain to me that the people playing his game—it wasn't anything Bethesda produced—were playing it wrong.

I immediately told him, 'they're not playing it wrong, they cannot play it wrong, it's their game. It's not yours anymore. However they are choosing to play it is the right way to play it'... If you embrace that on the developer side, you find yourself making all different kinds of content, both artistically and design, and for programming in terms of the systems that are available, so that everyone can play the game the way they want to".

I'm not sure I've ever heard a more succinct summation of the Bethesda school of game design than "You're not playing my game, I'm making your game". Accessibility, openness, a sanding down of edges that may scare off the normies (like ability scores and character classes—gone but not forgotten), and a general refusal to foreclose story branches or quest chains based on player decisions: these things are Bethesda to me.

In this maxim you find all the strengths and weaknesses of the studio's approach to open-world RPG design. On the one hand, the world is your oyster. If a questline is losing your interest, flip to another one. Don't like your build? Convert to something new. Bethesda's worlds are all-you-can-eat buffets and you have precisely zero dietary restrictions. True freedom!

And yet, and yet, to a certain kind of tedious grognard (me), it also leaves everything feeling a touch… limp—colourless in content and utterly unresponsive. You might be the head of every guild in the land and the bloodletter-in-chief of the local murder society, but the world is too shy to reply to it. After all, it can't. If your choices impacted things too hard you might experience a consequence, you might rub up against a rough edge, and then suddenly you might not be playing "your" game anymore.

#3972. Goddess of Victory: Nikke's PC launcher suffers potential malware infection, with its publishers suggesting folks who've booted since late September do a security check

A cruel twist for the Shift Up-developed epic shooter RPG of cruel humanity destiny

Goddess of Victory: Nikke, a gacha shooter/RPG developed by Stellar Blade makers Shift Up, has suffered a "security incident" which has seen its PC launcher potentially be infected with third-party malware. Thankfully, it seems a patch to make the launcher safe again has been quickly dished out, but publishers Level Infinite are still advising players who've booted the game up since September 27th to do some security checks.

"We have identified that some files in the NIKKE Windows PC launcher were recently tampered with by a third party, potentially allowing malicious programs to run when the launcher was launched," the developers of the game with anime girls who - judging by the promo art - breast boobily announced yesterday. "As a result, your PCs and account information may have been exposed to security risks.

"We are continuing to investigate the extent of the potential damage and review appropriate response measures. We are also conducting a thorough review of our network security environment, including our CDN, to determine how the PC launcher files were compromised. We will take all necessary precautions to prevent further damage and ensure that this issue does not happen again. We deeply regret that this security incident has caused Commanders significant concern and distress, when our responsibility should have been to provide a safe gaming environment."

In order to try and help players "scan for and remove the malicious programs distributed in this incident", publishers Level Infinite have added a feature to Nikke's official PC client that does just that. They're advising that anyone who's booted up the game at least once after September 27th at 15:41 (UTC+9) use that or perform a manual security check.

Once that's done, affected players are advised to change the passwords for any accounts they've used on the PC they used to boot the launcher, as well as generate new API keys and access tokens. "We take very seriously the possibility that this incident may have affected not only your gaming experience but also your PC, accounts with external services, and personal assets," Level Infinite added. "If you believe you may have been affected by this issue or suffered from any loss, please contact our customer support team. We will review each inquiry carefully and respond as promptly as possible."

Going forwards, they plan to improve their monitoring "so that any unauthorized file modifications or security threats can be detected early and addressed promptly", as well as "establish an integrity verification system for external resources accessed by the PC launcher" and ensure the launcher only requires "the minimum permissions necessary".

Here's hoping the studio are able to keep things more secure in the future and that affected players are able to get rid of any malware with minimal suffering or inconvenience.

#3971. Soulframe to launch into free open alpha this week, as Warframe devs go head-to-head with WoW: Forever

Soulframe's Preludes (its own version of an alpha) is finally opening its doors to the whole world ahead of the Verse of the Veilands update. Starting this week, anyone who wants to can simply download the game and hop in, no invite required.

The date this happens is an interesting one: 6th November. That's two days after the release of World of Warcraft: Forever and the same week as Old School RuneScape's Hardcore worlds, so it's suddenly become a pretty packed month for MMO enthusiasts.

This comes after three years of closed testing for the fantasy action MMORPG, which players have been able to gradually see firsthand through sporadic invites. With Soulframe suffering delays since its first reveal, brief invite events have already occurred over this period. Even locked away, the game has received multiple substantial updates over the years, including new quests, Pacts (classes), factions and so on.

As for what newcomers to Soulframe can look forward to when Soulframe opens its doors, the Verse of the Veillands update is bringing a total overhaul of the map progression system this month. After the completion of an early quest, players are introduced to a corrupted landscape, the Veillands, which they must purify.

As you do so, new resources will be obtainable and side activities like fishing will be unlocked. You'll also be able to train up a small wolf pet into a full-on mount in the process. Previously, players were just thrust into the open world to explore and figure things out as they go, so this should provide something of an introduction to the game's open map. It won't be totally finished when released mind you, with updates to the Veillands system coming in the future.

On top of that, there's a new Pact called the Ode Shrike coming with the update. It's a tricksy trapper with spikes, balloon snares, bombs and chains to disrupt enemies as you whittle them down.

Could this be enough to win people over to Digital Extreme's newest project? Time will tell - but in the meantime its long-lasting sci-fi MMO Warframe is taking players to the Tau system in a major next step in the game's narrative this December. It comes with a detective noir inspired main quest, playable warframe, and even an in-universe Poker equivalent.

#3970. Trails beyond the Horizon Sequel Confirmed for 2027 as Falcom Steps Back from Remakes

The next game in Falcom's long running Trails series will be a sequel to Trails beyond the Horizon.

The developer confirmed this in its annual financial report, putting to rest mass speculation from fans of the franchise.

First released in 2024 in Japan, Trails beyond the Horizon features world-shifting story revelations and ends on one hell of a cliffhanger. Its sequel should, finally, have all of the answers — and it's set to launch before the end of September 2027.

The wait hasn't been quite so bad for western players, as Horizon was localised back in January of this year.

However, it should be noted that Falcom's report only refers to the sequel's Japanese release.

It'll be up to western publisher NIS America to work out whether a global launch is feasible, but I'd be shocked if it's not on the cards, because this is the first time in history that the west is actually fully caught up on the series.

Of course, this also means that Falcom is stepping back from its remakes for the time being. After the huge success of Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter and Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter, there was a suggestion that the studio would simply follow the money, and go straight into remaking Trails in the Sky the 3rd.

But it's no secret that the developer is ramping up towards the end of Trails as a whole — and so it's prioritising the next step in the franchise's current saga.

Falcom says that Horizon's sequel is the only major title it has in the works for 2027. As such, it's highly likely that its next remake will be targeting a 2028 release.

With all of this in mind, we should be getting our first look at Horizon's sequel in the coming months.

Capcom's modern Resident Evil remakes are fantastic entry points for one of the most beloved survival horror series of all time, but it's always felt weird that the very first 1996 game still hasn't been given the full-blown third-person RE Engine treatment. Yes, there's a remake from 2002, but it's way more faithful to the original game than the much more recent remakes of Resident Evil 2, 3, and 4, featuring the classic tank controls and static camera from the series' origin. Basically, if you want to start Resident Evil with the first game in the series, you have to deal with quite a few design foundations that'll feel seriously dated if you're unfamiliar. Like ink ribbons. You don't want ink ribbons, trust me.

With how successful the Resident Evil remakes have been, it may seem inevitable that Capcom revisits the very first game. But while rumors suggest there's already a new RE1 early in development, there's been no official announcement or even heavily substantiated reporting to add weight to those rumors. As to why Capcom didn't choose Resident Evil as the obvious starting point for its newer remakes, longtime series producer Jun Takeuchi says the company worried it wouldn't resonate with a modern audience.

"The reason we didn't choose Resident Evil 1 as the first remake is because it's such a stoic game," Takeuchi says in a new book celebrating the series' 30th anniversary (translation via Fandom). "Because it focuses so heavily on the horror derived from its stoicism, we were concerned that it might not resonate with today's game fans."

As is always the case with second-hand translations, it's hard to pin down the exact intent behind translated words like "stoic," but Resident Evil 1 definitely has a distinct vibe and slower pace than newer games in the series. Speaking of which, Takeuchi says the iconic opening sequence from Resident Evil 2, which sets up the mass infection of Raccoon City, is basically where everything kicks off anyway.

"Furthermore, the Raccoon City incident is essentially the starting point of the Resident Evil saga, so we felt that experiencing that was the best way to introduce the origins," he says.

I definitely don't disagree. Resident Evil 2 is arguably the most classic version of Resident Evil you can experience, whether that's the 1998 original or the 2019 remake. That said, as a lifelong fan and noted tank control hater, I would love to see a modern reimagining of the game that started it all.

Where does your favorite land on our ranking of the best Resident Evil games?

#3968. "We're doing great," says id Software boss, despite losing "about half of our studio" amid devastating Xbox cuts

Iconic Doom and Quake developer id Software was among the most heavily impacted Microsoft-owned studios during Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating business "reset" earlier this year, with around 136 employees reportedly losing their jobs.

In the wake of those layoffs, id Software co-studio director Marty Stratton was recently asked about the current state of the developer, and how it has been affected by Sharma's cuts. "We're doing great," Stratton told journalists at a recent event (via IGN).

"Not to handwave the [layoffs] away… everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that," he continued. "But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and technology department."

This is not the first time a senior id Software member has pushed back on the narrative the studio has been "nerfed into the ground and gutted". Hugo Martin, id's other co-studio head previously claimed the remaining team is "the size we were when we made Doom 2016, and id Tech is very much alive and well".

Sharma's Xbox reset will ultimately see 3,200 jobs cut across Microsoft's gaming division, with many of those still to come. Those impacted by the first wave of cuts in July, however, included developers working on the id Software's id Tech engine. This is the engine behind all of the studio's games, and is known to be among the most performant engines, consistently producing visually-impressive games that require modest specs to run.

Following the layoffs, many inside and outside the studio said the id Tech team had been gutted. Longtime id Software programmer Chris Hays, who notably wasn't among those let go, said at the time, "It is hard to make a game that is triple-A, that is like we've done before, with half the people. And by hard I mean impossible". Hays also claimed "entire departments" and "entire disciplines" are gone.

While Stratton hasn't addressed those comments directly, he revealed id Software is now "working more closely than ever" with MachineGames, the Swedish studio behind the modern Wolfenstein games, and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. "We've always had a very close partnership with [MachineGames], but I think we're at a point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]," he explained.

"We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that. We're both really really bullish on what we have ahead."

Id Software's next project remains unclear. MachineGames, on the other hand, recently said it's not done with Wolfenstein, so it's possible a sequel to 2017's The New Colossus is in the works.

#3967. Nvidia ensure unboxing a ludicrously expensive new graphics card isn't limited to real life in these RAM crisis times by releasing a GeForce 8800 GTX unpacking sim

Hey at least the card in this bit of 2006 nostalgia bait has only cost you a virtual arm and leg

In what feels a fairly cheeky move during a time when memory shortages have infamously made it pretty much impossible to buy a decently powerful new graphics card without spending approximately a gazillion pounds/dollars/dollarpounds, Nvidia have decided to put out a Steam demo that allows folks to re-live the feeling of unboxing a ludicrously expensive graphics card in 2006.

The demo, dubbed GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend, has been developed by Dylan Browne. He previously made Through The Ages, a "real-time high end graphical cinematic that takes us on a nostalgic journey through three of NVIDIA's iconic GPUs" which is also on Steam for reasons.

The GeForce 8800 GTX demo, as you might've guessed, is a tribute to that specific card in the form of a tech demo simulating what it was like to unbox one in a mid-2000s bedroom. Seriously, there's a copy of Crysis on the desk so you know this is the domain of a true devotee to the best graphics available in around 2007.

"Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower," the demo's description declares. "Explore nods to GeForce history and hidden easter eggs as DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry bring the nostalgic setting to life. From holding the card to the glow of the monitor, rediscover a moment in PC gaming history - or experience it for the first time!"

As the GeForce 8800 GTX was a top-line card that cost $599 on release in 2006 - about $1,000 in today's money if the online inflation calculator I've just used is on the money - this isn't really a 'we know cards are ludicrously expensive right now, but here's a reminder of when you used to be able to actually afford to unbox one' sort of demo. It is at least a free way to virtually experience having blown a chunk of your savings on something that can render really sexy textures without the existential dread of doing so in real life.

Well, I say that, I've just noticed the minimum requirements for the demo note that you'll need an RTX 4070 card. So, depending on your current setup, this might well be a case of Nvidia offering the chance to render unboxing a card you couldn't afford in 2006 via a card you can't afford in 2026.

Is that about the best we can all hope for in 2026? Probably.

Last Friday, the very good RPG Nier: Automata underwent what the scientific community calls 'puffer-fishification'. That is to say, it suddenly and inexplicably ballooned to over 700% of its original download size, as an update magically transformed the game from a reedy 50 GB lightweight into a 366-GB behemoth.

But it has since hit the Ozempic and is now back down to its regular size. "We have identified the cause and now resolved this issue," tweeted the official Nier X account earlier today. "Apologies for any inconvenience caused."

Notably absent from the bugfix notice was any explanation as to just what had happened. It might be academic at this point, but I for one would love to know how you accidentally make a game seven times bigger without anything changing.

Squenix is keeping schtum, but Rick Lane suggested, in our article last week about the bug, that it might have been related to Nier: Automata's DLC packages. "When selected for download on Steam, each DLC appears to have the same file size as the base game", he noted. "Weirdly though, this is only true for the initial download and installation. Once the game is installed, the file reportedly reverts to a more appropriate size of roughly 50 gigs." Indeed, the suggested temporary workaround for the issue (before Square Enix fixed it) was to uncheck all the DLCs when you installed the game.

So it sure seems like, somehow, the base files for the entire original game got attached to each individual DLC package. That might also explain why the size increase only applied to the downloads and not its install size—the whole game got downloaded eight times, but it was simply overwriting the base game files over and over.

That's just my speculation though, and without more news from Squenix, that's all we're gonna get. For now, enjoy being able to once again download 2B and 9S' adventures without having to start the download two weeks in advance.

#3965. Apex Legends adds a grumpy, teamwiping Godzilla to its growing history of unappealing crossovers

No doubt eager as peas to help pay off EA's billions in debt, battle royale shooter Apex Legends is set to run another of its intellectual propertytastic crossover events. This one, starting on November 10th, stars Godzilla, of Godzilla Minus Zero, Godzilla vs. Kong, Godzilla (1954), Godzilla 2000: Millennium, Godzilla (1998), Son of Godzilla, and Godzilla (2014). I might be missing some.

Besides a profitable range of weapon and character skins, most of which appear to have hot glue gunned an 70-year film franchise's worth of dorsal fins all over themselves, the King of the Monsters himself will show up on the game's Storm Point map. He does at least have more than a background cameo: he'll occasionally blast an area with Legend-melting atomic breath, though brave souls who risk the danger zone can score a custom Devotion LMG with a unique heat ray attack of its own.

Worth noting also that the character skins are each based on a certain 'zilla movie, though as our freelance news writer and associate Large Lizard Cinema expert Ashley isn't working today, I'm not sure which of these are from hits and which are the duds. Walking wallhack motherfucker Bloodhound gets the newest fashion, their skin being inspired by Minus Zero, while my personal favourite Scottish scientist Horizon gets duds based on Big G in Godzilla vs. Destoroyah. Octane's skin is taken from... something called a Jet Jaguar? Google suggests this may in fact be elite Godzilla knowledge, something I clearly lack.

Regardless, and with the understanding that a lot of effort goes into these crossovers, I still kinda wish they didn't exist? Even putting aside basic game-playing problems with how, for example, wacky skins interfere with Legend silhouettes – you couldn't pay me to initiate a fight against a full team of near-identical Gundampeople - it's just icky to have an otherwise sharp, smart, at times fiercely competitive battle royale turned into an animated billboard for a few days.

Besides, Apex already has its own kaiju: the sleepy, pacifist Leviathans that innocently wandered into the King's Canyon map for a few of the earlier seasons. I consider these much better Friend Material than Godzilla, on the grounds that they'd only kill you by accident, and it was usually your own fault - by wandering under their briefly raised megahooves - anyway.

#3964. Over a decade later, Bloodborne remains so popular it reportedly sold a quarter of a million copies this year alone

Bloodborne, FromSoftware's singular Lovecraftian action-RPG, has reportedly sold more than 251,000 copies this year alone.

That's according to Alinea Analytics head of market analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed the figure in a post on X, noting this brings Bloodborne's total sales up to an estimated 10.4m copies, generating $317m (around £236m) in revenue. Elliot also claimed more than half a million people played Bloodborne in October through PlayStation Plus.

Additionally, 12 percent of those are said to have played Elden Ring during the month, while 6 percent played Dark Souls 3, and 5 percent played Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. There's a cohort of gamers who are always bouncing between different From[Software] games," Elliott pointed out. "Can't blame them, especially with this one."

Bloodborne is a PlayStation exclusive that sadly never left the PS4, despite consistent calls from fans for ports and remasters. While the game is playable on PS5 through backwards compatibility, Bloodborne barely benefits from the console's advanced hardware, only seeing smoother frame pacing. In other words, it's the same game with barely any perceptible upgrades.

Before Sony closed down Demon's Souls remake developer Bluepoint Games earlier this year, the studio reportedly pitched a Bloodborne remake, but original developer FromSoftware didn't want it to happen. When news of the pitch came to light, former Sony Interactive Entertainment Shuhei Yoshida said Bloodborne has a special place in director Hidetaka Miyazaki's heart and speculated the reason it hasn't had a remake is because Miyazaki would prefer to do it himself but doesn't have the time.

"Miyazaki-san really, really loved Bloodborne, what he created," Yoshida said at the time. "So I think he is interested but he's so successful and he's so busy, so he cannot do it himself, and he doesn't want anyone else to touch it."

Sony's trail of bodies is only getting longer

Sony has dug up another plot in its expanding live-service graveyard, and is lowering the still-warm corpse of Haven Studios' Fairgames into the dirt. The shooter, which was revealed in 2023, has been canceled, though PlayStation says there will be no layoffs as a result of its decision to end the project.

"The studio will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities," a PlayStation representative tells Bloomberg, who first reported the news.

Fairgames was revealed in a 2023 trailer which stylized the title as "Fairgame$." The trailer featured no in-game footage, but presented a stylish version of a Payday-style shooter focused on heists. But the game never materialized again. The last major news on the project came in 2025, when Haven Studios founder Jade Raymond – a veteran Ubisoft producer who'd worked on Assassins' Creed – left the company.

Bloomberg reports that Fairgames was ultimately canceled after a poor showing during a recent test session with thousands of players. "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," according to an internal memo.

PlayStation had apparently reworked the game multiple times since it was first revealed, and prior to the test had planned to showcase it again under a new title, according to the report.

While PlayStation once had extensive plans for live-service games, it's canceled so many of those projects that it's now difficult to keep track of them all. The death of Concord just two weeks after launch is perhaps the highest profile example, but that's just the most memorable corpse among an extensive trail of bodies.

A multiplayer God of War title from Bluepoint and a live-service game from Bend Studio were canceled in 2025. A multitude of unannounced projects were iced amid mass layoffs at PlayStation in 2024, including a Twisted Metal game and an original project from the publisher's now-defunct London studio. Naughty Dog's The Last of Us multiplayer game died in 2023. Bungie has reportedly had numerous projects scrapped since it was acquired by Sony. PlayStation has even killed not just one, but two projects helmed by Call of Duty veteran Jason Blundell.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Sony's biggest live-service hit in recent years is certainly Helldivers 2, but it's struggled to replicate that success – heck, it's struggled to release other online games at any scale. The publisher's annual MLB The Show series remains a staple among baseball fans, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls seems to have found a niche among fighting game aficionados, and Marathon is continuing to survive, but these aren't the Fortnite-level hits Sony is clearly gunning for. I guess we'll never know whether Fairgames could've been a hit.

#3962. As the controversy around AI-created video game copies continues, Anthropic seemingly restricts Claude's cloning abilities

An update to Anthropic's Claude AI software has seemingly blocked the creation of outright clones or copies of existing games. Instead, Claude has been altered to only create "original" games.

Among the first to share news of the change was X user Chasm, who posted a screenshot showing the new rule, purportedly added around 27th October. "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets," it reads. "Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”.

While Anthropic is yet to issue an official statement on the new rule, technical staff member Addy Osmani commented beneath Chasm's post, confirming the change's legitimacy. He noted it was included because "using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy", but added that creating original games and those built with a user's own assets should still be possible.

Following the new rule's inclusion, users on GitHub shared newfound barriers they'd run into as a result. Reports included being blocked from creating digital modules for board games, and from recreating a commercially produced board game for personal use. Eurogamer has contacted Anthropic for comment on the rule change and its stance on AI game copies.

The modifications to Claude have appeared at a time when AI copies of games have drawn increasing ire, with game communities pushing back against them and developers pulling public-facing demos in fear of having their work stolen. AI-assisted copies of triple-A games have also emerged, including a version of Mario Kart 8 playable in an internet browser. However, this was taken down in a matter of days, presumably thanks to a legal notice from Nintendo.

Of course, even if Claude is prevented from making game copies, other AI tools, such as Deepseek, still lack similar restrictions. Until such measures are ubiquitous, the issue will continue. Given Claude's position as one of the most popular commercial AI tools out there, however, this will certainly make a dent in the problem.

#3961. The Legend of Khiimori's Mongolian Expanse update brings in frosty mountains and scorching deserts that'll require a lot more than a fur coat and a sturdy horse

Another day, another opportunity for some horsing around! I'm being literal here, to be clear, as a new update for The Legend of Khiimori dropped yesterday. It's called The Mongolian Expanse, opening up the map a whole lot more and making a sweep of other additions to the game.

Previously, you might have looked out unto the snowy mountainscapes and the scorching deserts and thought "boy howdy am I glad I can't go there, those temperatures look like a nightmare to deal with!" Well, good news, as you now can head to those locales, each with "their own waystations, Yam nodes, named places, chests and bandit caches."

You don't want to wander there without some amount of prep, however, as the mountains are cold and difficult to climb, with wolves none too kind to humans like you. The desert, of course, is really hot, for both you and your horse. Both additions remind me of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and its use of extreme temperatures acting as a sort of challenge gate. Neat stuff!

The buck doesn't stop there with this update though. You'll find a whole host of new wildlife, ranging from wild boars, to gobi bears and camels. Of course, a horse game wouldn't be one without more horse, which there is! It's a new breed called the Marwari, a horse that is "built for endurance and especially resistant to heat, a strong partner for long, punishing Desert crossings." Beyond that, you'll also find more than 60 new horse skills, all findable across specific regions and for specific breeds.

It's a nice beefy update with plenty more tweaks, additions and fixes on top of everything mentioned above. When it comes to the mountains and desert, you can also expect some big additions there, as this is only the first part of this update. You can read about everything else the update offers right here on Steam.

#3960. Try Hellraiser: Revival in This New PS5 Demo, Out Now

Saber Interactive is letting you sample the opening moments of Hellraiser: Revival via a new PS5 demo that's been put on the PS Store today. This isn't one that's tied to PS Plus Premium; it's a free download for everyone.

You'll get to play through the game's prologue, and then a "portion" of the first chapter. This means you'll get to see a lot of what the title is all about: gore, action, sex... and more gore. The first hour or so lets you enter the Labyrinth, and then chapter one is more of a stealth sequence where you have to escape your captors.

Since the demo breaks up a piece of the full game, I don't believe that your progress would carry over if you were to buy it afterwards. Still, it's a nice sample of a horror game I had a lot of fun with a few weeks ago.

Opinion Hey, That Hellraiser: Revival Game Is Pretty Good

If you like what you play, Hellraiser: Revival is full price at the moment: £34.99 / $39.99 on the PS Store. I expect the game will go on sale at some point before the year is out, though, so it might be worth waiting and keeping an eye on our coverage of the PS Store sales to come.

Will you give the new Hellraiser: Revival demo on PS5 a go? Let us know in the comments below.

I've spent far too much of my life covering the rampant ascent of AI. A juggernaut of tech development, destined to change the world into some sort of sci-fi utopia (if you believe its advocates) or fated to come crashing down around our ears, taking a large chunk of the world economy with it. Or the end of the world as we know it, according to some.

And now, the pillars upon which the AI revolution sits seem to be shaking beneath it. The most recent tremors began with the wobbling of US AI-led tech stocks in mid-October, after a similar descent in China earlier this year. Then at the end of the month, while many tech companies reported huge amounts of revenue in their quarterly financial results, some AI tech share prices still slid under a black cloud of investor doubt.

None more so than Alphabet, the owner of Google. A $500 billion wipe in stock price, led by the admission that the company's own AI search features were eating into its ad revenue, rocked the market. A wider tech sell-off, fuelled by fears regarding the eventual profitability of AI and a potential upcoming Democrat victory in the US midterms, rattled the valuations of many AI tech companies—alongside the chip manufacturers sitting underneath them.

All this, of course, amid a backdrop of increasing AI-related concerns across multiple fields. Rogue AI agents. Increasing AI-powered cybersecurity incidents. Predictions of the end of civilisation, brought on by rampant AI development without proper oversight. Fears of job market ruination. AI psychosis. The list goes on.

Then, the so-called blue wave came to pass. Democrats won control of both the US House and the Senate. Such sweeping political changes can rarely be ascribed to a single factor, but US voter polling indicates that data center expansion was a key source of voter frustration. The current Republican administration has gone all in on AI, and much of the US public seems displeased at the idea of massive AI tech facilities springing up left, right, and center across the country.

Jensen Huang has hit the headlines over allegations surrounding his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trillions were wiped off US tech stock values as investors sold off increasing numbers of shares in tech companies, amid further fears that the great AI infrastructure buildout was about to be reigned in by political changes. Long-called-for regulation of AI and AI companies seemed—and indeed, still seems—ever more likely.

And now, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has hit the headlines over allegations surrounding his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy. At first, it was reported that Alice Huang (no relation) had a "close relationship" with the Nvidia chief.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Now, Jensen Huang has himself admitted that the two were engaged in an affair, and Nvidia has launched an internal investigation into concerns related to national security. The timing could not be worse for the US tech market. At the time of writing, Nvidia's share value has sunk in pre-market trading.

The company is, in many ways, the backbone of the AI revolution, the chief provider of the chips behind the sweeping AI rollout that has changed the tech landscape over the past few years, and the creator of the CUDA platform that underpins it. Huang is its charismatic leader, the relentless optimist behind this AI-led future we're supposedly about to enjoy. A scandal at this stage is likely the last thing any tech investor wants to see.

So, what now? While the long-mooted AI bubble burst has yet to materialise in full, it's certainly looking like the relentless "all the money in the world" optimism phase is coming to an end. Investors are shaken, with worries about long-term profitability continuing to eat into the market, alongside US national security concerns now dominating the headlines.

The train with no brakes is rocking wildly against the tracks—and unfortunately, given AI and big tech's role in the global economy, we're all stuck in the carriages behind it.

The relentless "all the money in the world" optimism phase is coming to an end.

I'm no economist. I can't tell you if this is the beginning of the AI bubble pop, or whether this is merely an extremely turbulent time in the AI success story. Certainly, it seems like the horse has already bolted, and that AI is here to stay in some form or fashion. Those hoping for a return to the good old, pre-AI days are almost certain to be disappointed.

But, having reported on so many "AI doomsayers" over the past few years, I can tell you that a fall from grace has been predicted by many. Such a massive, world-changing technological development, fuelled by seemingly impossible amounts of investment, has always seemed destined to face some sort of financial reckoning.

That reckoning, I believe, has never looked closer. May you live in interesting times, as the old saying goes. And what happens next? Well, it's going to be interesting, at the very least.

#3958. One World of Warcraft: Forever player is working on a first-person mod that's a love letter to retro RPGs like Hexen and Morrowind

One World of Warcraft: Forever player is attempting to turn Blizzard's new MMO endeavour into a Morrowind-esque first-person fantasy RPG, full of retro animations harkening back to the good ol' days. And there's no generative AI in sight.

The project, known as Retro Forever, is the work of modder Arhkain, who's so far published two dev vlogs detailing the nature of his work. He opens the first vlog by describing how he always wanted to view the world of Azeroth through his character's eyes, but was met with a lack of adequate options to support this style of play. That encouraged him to find his own solutions, which is how Retro Forever was born.

The result is a WoW Forever mod aiming to incorporate "fully immersive" first-person graphics - whether it be for combat, cooking, or flying across the world - with a presentation style reminiscent of classic first-person fantasy games like Morrowind or Hexen. In fact, the mod currently uses assets pulled and modified from those games.

Retro Forever - which is described as a "clever combination of addons that already exist" - includes a custom user interface, as well as animations attached to specific spells and abilities. That means, if you're a mage and attack an enemy with a spell, you'll see a custom animation of your character doing that spell.

The bad news is the mod isn't publicly available right now, and currently only works with a selection of mage spells and other class abilities. However, that's set to expand - and Arhkain recently revealed an artist has expressed interest in joining the project for original asset creation.

As for the no-generative AI deal, Arhkain said the tool "wouldn't help" in the mod's development. And when Retro Forever has been updated with original art to replace its currently borrowed assets, it should also dodge any legal pitfalls too. Nice!

With World of Warcraft: Forever set to release this Wednesday, 4th November, excitement is abound for the new spin on an old MMO. Judging from my time with the beta, the game is looking rather good!

#3957. After a 16-year long dev period, Faraway, a shooting star arcade game about siphoning the energy of other stars, is out now

Lord almighty, video games take a while to make, 'ey? Especially if you're just one person working on it by yourself. Such is the case with Faraway, out today, an arcade game that reminds me of the early days of PS3 indies "about a shooting star that creates constellations to stay alive," all made single-handedly by creator of cult-classic mobile game Eliss, Steph Thirion. Did I mention that Faraway took 16 years to make? Like I said, game development is a lengthy process.

Looking at Faraway, and knowing how long it took to produce, it doesn't surprise me to come from a dev who managed to release a mobile game in the early days of the platform, long before free-to-play got its chokehold on the industry. It also really does feel like it should be sitting amongst the likes of PixelJunk, this thing should be something I'm desperate to play on my PS3 while I wait for my controller to charge.

As mentioned, you are a shooting star, a "spark meant to shine and vanish in a blink." But still you persist, connecting to and wrapping yourself around starts to "harvest their energy," in turn lengthening your own life, and of course, in arcadey fashion, racking up a nice score. It looks like game design as poetry, everything you're looking at procedurally generated to bring freshness to every run. I can fully envision this as a "one more run" kind of arcade game, the best kind, especially in an age long past the need to shove in another of your hard earned coins.

Faraway conceptually charms me because it taps into a style of game we don't get to see much of any more. What I'm saying is, I'm just a teensy bit sick of how many roguelikes there are, but that doesn't mean I don't want a game I can just hop in and out of at my own whims. Sure, arcade games might not be in vogue, I just miss them a bit. In any case, Faraway is available to pick up on Steam right now. Seems like it'll be worth a punt!

Thankfully, Skyward Sword's director says "no hard feelings"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is, by most standards, a pretty faithful remake to the original game, but Nintendo wasn't scared to make changes where necessary. I was a little bummed to learn the fun references to the Super Mario Bros. series had been removed, not to mention some Zelda: Skyward Sword art that was in the Ocarina of Time 3DS remake, but with how carefully Nintendo positions every game, remaster, and remake into its existing portfolio, I'm not at all surprised.

In case you aren't a Zelda historian, the original game has several Mario references including character portraits and heavy design influences on characters like Talon, Malon, and Ingo, who strongly resemble Mario, Peach, and Luigi, respectively. It makes a lot of sense as Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Super Mario 64 were both being made at the same time, but 30 years later, the remake doesn't share that same connection to Mario 64. That's why the portraits have been removed from the remake, even though it's still pretty clear Talon, Malon, and Ingo have doppelgangers hanging out in the Mario universe.

"Certainly, at the time, when we put those there, I don't think anybody thought it was too big a deal. Maybe there was a more carefree or comfortable approach to that sort of thing," Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma tells Game Informer. "But looking at it now, like if a player is coming through that area, and given the overall way that we're, you know, creating this world and giving the player that form of expression, if they look up and they think, 'Why is Yoshi there?' We don't want that moment to interrupt their experience of the world in that way. So we're feeling a little bit differently about it this time."

Similarly to the original Ocarina of Time and Mario 64, 3DS Ocarina of Time released around the same time as Zelda: Skyward Sword, which explains the crossover references there. And likewise, they were removed from the new Ocarina of Time remake so as not to distract from everything else going on.

"I do remember at the time the designers on the 3DS version were really interested in placing Easter Eggs like that throughout the game, and the timing of the release of Skyward Sword was such that it was perfect to go ahead and include that. So I said, 'Okay, sure,'" says Aonuma, but same as before with the Mario 64 references, "you don't want to interrupt the player's experience by seeing something that's unrelated to what they're currently doing in the game. So for that reason, we decided not to go that way."

Game Informer was kind enough to consider the feelings of Skyward Sword director Hidemaro Fujibayashi, who took part in the same interview, but thankfully it's all water under the bridge.

"It's really as Mr. Aonuma said. There was an underlying concept in what we were going for, so no hard feelings there," he says.

#3955. Ablahshikar is a maximalist, sickos only salvage-survival CRPG about ripping organs out of warships and pawning off strange goods that's now out in early access

I don't know what's going on, and I like it

Sometimes, you come across a game and instantly know it's for the sickos. Today that is Ablahshikar, a "turn-based salvage-survival CRPG adrift on the Candle Sea" where you rip out the organs of enemy warships to "rebuild your vessel into a doomed chimera," that is out now in early access. To be honest I could have just called it a CRPG and still labelled it as a game for sickos, yet everything that's going on here is obviously just doubling down on the sick factor.

Ablahshikar is a particular flavour of maximalism. Having not played it, it feels a bit impossible describe, I mean, just have a read of some of the game's Steam page: "Lo, destiny crooks a finger only to those whose eyes peer beyond þe next tempest. Take custody of a faltering war-barge that wanders the outer brine of Dastgerd. Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." I don't know what any of that means! And I love it. Reminds me of Hylics in that the game's world is not translating itself for its audience; you take what you're given, and you figure it out yourself.

Judging from trailers and screenshots, there's a mix of activities to be getting on with. Occasionally you'll be piloting a strange, not alien, but definitely ancient ship of some kind in an arcadey sort of fashion. Then occasionally there's something that resembles Caves of Qud, i.e. some odd, 2D maybe dungeon crawling where your moves are dictated by individual keys on your keyboard. Then there's Disco Elysiumy cutscenes that feel like a video game designed in the year 1200 by someone from the year 2200, aesthetically anyway. As I said, it is a particular flavour of maximalism.

Truthfully, I do not know if I am sicko enough for Ablahshikar. Its mighty vision is terrifying, but I certainly am curious about it. Right now it's less than a fiver, and it'll only be in early access for roughly a couple of months where the price will then go up, so perhaps it's best to get in at the ground floor. If you are one such sicko, then you can pick it up on Steam right here.

#3954. COD Modern Warfare 4 has seemingly answered DMZ players' PvE calls with new Story Mission changes - but there are major caveats

For as long as Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction mode has been available, there've been calls for PvE-only servers. Developer Infinity Ward, for its part, has maintained the mode is designed as a PvPvE experience, but it's now seemingly made a change offering solo players something of a compromise, albeit with caveats.

In DMZ, your choice of deployment type dictates the matchmaking pool you're put into. You can choose to freely roam the map, picking up tasks as you go, or participate in slightly more structured Dynamic Ops which constantly generate tasks for you to do. But DMZ also has Story Missions, a title that suggests they're private instances. But that wasn't the case at launch. Although the number of players allowed into Story Mission instances appeared to be smaller than in other modes, it was still possible to run into other players, which meant potentially unwanted PvP encounters.

Now, however, Infinity Ward appears to have made Story Missions private, but only for solo players, and only when playing a Story Mission for the first time - after which, repeated attempts will be much less forgiving.

Infinity Ward has not officially announced a change, but players began noticing it on Reddit and elsewhere, and I wanted to investigate for myself: I just finished a Story Mission - a first attempt - and despite making as much noise as possible, I ran into no other players. The Recent Players list in the social tab, which displays the names of players you've recently crossed paths with, was likewise empty for me. I also noticed zero activated UAV Towers and SAM Sites - a rare sight in PvPvE matches where players always run to the former to reveal enemies around them. There's some suggestion you may still run into others in a Story Mission, however, so best not lower your guard. As welcome as the change is, it highlights the split in DMZ's community. Many would rather not cross paths with other players, and it's especially frustrating for those expecting a purely PvE mode in this year's Call of Duty.

Friends, it's once again time to set sail on the stormy seas of democracy and answer a vital question: which are the best games of 2026 according to a set of 22 distinct categories? Also there are three other categories, but they're chosen by judges and not the public, so it's less the stormy seas of democracy and more the technocratic autobahn of experience-based decision-making.

It's time for the Golden Joystick Awards 2026 Presented by Pot Noodle, is what I'm saying, and you (yes, you) are invited to watch when the big show airs at 10 am PT / 1 pm ET / 6 pm GMT / 7 pm CEST on Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

This year's host is Alix Wilton Regan, most recently the voice of Lara Croft in Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, but most notably for me the voice of Alt Cunningham in Cyberpunk 2077, Specialist Traynor in Mass Effect 3, and Loghain's lieutenant Cauthrien in Dragon Age: Origins. Real heads know.

The show goes out on every streaming platform you've heard of and perhaps a few you haven't. You can watch the ceremony live via YouTube, Twitch, Steam, TikTok and X as well as Future Games Show, PC Gamer, WhatCulture Gaming, IGN, Ginx TV, eClutch, Niconico, Kuaishou and Bilibili.

There are a whole bunch of games in the running for the GJAs numerous gongs, and I genuinely don't know which of them will come out ahead. We've got 007 First Light, Big Walk, Crimson Desert, Control Resonant, Dispatch, Forza Horizon 6, Meccha Chamelon, Mewgenics, Resident Evil Requiem, and plenty more. It's a gamut of games—a game-ut—and you'll have to tune in to see which ones go home with their arms heaving with trophies.

#3952. BioWare are gone, but at least you'll be able to watch their final days in a documentary next year and oh wait that's really sad actually

It feels like every single week for the past few years has been the infinitely quotable 30 Rock quote on repeat. That feeling struck particularly last month when EA decided to shut down the iconic Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare. That obviously resulted in the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, of which a leaked trailer and some, now former, devs made sound pretty interesting. But hey! At least there's a documentary coming next year all about the studio that managed to capture the studio's last days! Yeah, I'm not so convinced by this upside either.

As reported by Deadline, Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie will be helming a documentary about the beloved RPG studio for Canada's Super Channel. It's called, punnily enough, Massive Effect: The BioWare Story, and will apparently take a look at its origins in 1995 all the way up to its closure and a bit beyond, planned for release in 2027. Filming began two years ago, so clearly this was meant to be much more of a celebratory project than the funeral procession it's going to be.

Some big names from BioWare's history will be appearing in the doc, including its founders Ray Muzyka, Greg Zeschuk and Augustine Yip, alongside the likes of longtime devs like Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Drew Karpyshyn, Aaryn Flynn, Mac Walters, Trent Oster, James Ohlen and Caroline Livingstone. You can also expect appearances from Jennifer Hale, Casey Hudson and, as if his sole goal is to haunt this industry everywhere, Geoff Keighley.

In a statement, co-founders Muzyka and Zeschuk said, "When the production team asked for our blessing to tell the BioWare story, we were honored and deeply moved. BioWare was never just about the logo or the building. It was about the stories brought to life by the amazing people on our dev teams, and the fans who defended those worlds, championed them and carried them forward. We’re proud this film honors those who made it all possible. The best stories never really end. They live on in our memories and wait for someone to pick them up again."

Obviously the documentary won't only be about the studio's closure, it sounds like a much bigger effort than that, so hopefully it will be a way to recognise how much of an influence BioWare has had on RPGs. It's just a ridiculous shame that it's something of a posthumous release. Continued solidarity with all those at BioWare.

#3951. Nintendo tried adding fast travel to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, before devs realised "we were missing out on the moments of discovery"

"I thought we needed to address this in this new version."

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is being wrapped up in all kinds of modern touches for its imminent Nintendo Switch 2 remake (that owl seems to be less chatty, for starters), but there's at least one quality-of-life feature borrowed from Breath of the Wild that the developers felt was better left on the cutting room floor: fast travel.

In Nintendo's latest Ask The Developer blog post, long-time series producer Eiji Aonuma explained that he initially asked the game's remakers to add warp points so players could get around Hyrule without having to spam rolls and presumably make Link violently ill in the process. But he and the team quickly realised fast travel doesn't work so well in a game that's still, in its bones, almost three decades old.

"In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, there are many warp points that enable players to move quickly around the game's vast world. In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry," Aonuma said.

"I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didn't exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, 'Wait, what's this?' Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again."

There you have it. No fast-travel points in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake, and it sounds like it's for the best. I avoided warping around Breath of the Wild's open world for the same reasons Aonuma laid out - spotting something odd way in the distance, slowly finding a way to reach it, and then discovering a funky little Korok seed was always a thrill that wouldn't have been possible by cutting out the trek in between main objectives.

Talking about why Nintendo chose to revive Ocarina of Time now, Aonuma said some of the younger developers on the team had maybe never played the original game 28 years ago, and remaking it could "trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development."

As for the remake's somewhat divisive art style, art director Aya Shida said the team "used phrases like 'a puppet-show feel' and 'the analog feel of practical effects films'" early on in production. "Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds," Shida continued.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time comes out on the 5th of November. After getting some hands-on time with the revival, Lottie thought it was shaping up to be a brilliant remake.

#3949. Take on a time-manipulating corporation in the very Soul Eater meets Jet Set Radio action roguelite CHRONO PUNK

Plus a little bit of Spider-Man, Devil May Cry and Kingdom Hearts

My favourite kind of game that's obviously going for the vibe of a particular era of gaming is one that doesn't look like it's trying to be any other game from said era, moreso if someone told me it was a PS2 or a Dreamcast game everyone forgot about I'd believe you. CHRONO PUNK fits that vibe quite well, an action roguelite that looks like it's taking some cues from those aforementioned consoles, alongside the likes of Soul Eater, Jet Set Radio, Devil May Cry, and Spider-Man.

That is, obviously, a lot of things, but CHRONO PUNK on the surface appears to have its own identity at least. Your player character looks like an almost nightcore version of Sora Kingdom Hearts, with various roles and weapons to choose from; there's a sword and shield, pistols, shurikon, grimoire, and most Soul Eatery of all, a scythe. CHRONO PUNK's got vibes, too. The cities you do combat in are big and nondescript when it comes to details, but ripe for jetting about and Spider-Man-style swinging across the place. And besides, it looks like there's some hub areas ripped straight out of any stylised MMO from the 2000s.

I'm liking the look of the combat too. This'll obviously be one for the combo pilled out there, people who like to bounce back and forth between their enemies like a pinball. Slow paced, this is not. Sick, I hope this is. Pair all of that with some bouncy, wall running movement, and there's some real potential for a strong game here. Sounds like you'll be able to play it in co-op or solo too, which is a nice touch.

The story doesn't seem all that complicated, with some mega corporation manipulating time thereby controlling the city and the masses, leaving you to deal with the mess, but hey, I'm here for the vibes. As of right now, there's no release date attached to CHRONO PUNK, but you can wishlist it on Steam while you wait.
